chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — London. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [The King, Lord John of Lancaster, the Earl of Westmoreland and others enter.]

KING. Shaken and pale with worry as we are, let’s find a moment for frightened peace to catch her breath. Then, still short of breath, she can announce new battles, to be started on shores far away. This land will no longer thirstily smear her lips with her own children’s blood. War will no longer cut trenches across her fields or crush her flowers under the hooves of enemy horses. Those opposing armies were like meteors in a stormy sky, all of one nature and born of one substance. Until lately they clashed in the shock of civil war, in the furious hand-to-hand of slaughter among countrymen. Now they will march together, in orderly, well-matched ranks, all in one direction. They will no longer fight against friends, relatives and allies. The blade of war, like a badly sheathed knife, will no longer cut its own master. So, friends, we will now raise an English army and lead it as far as Christ’s tomb. We are his soldiers now, enlisted and sworn to fight under his blessed cross. Our men were shaped in their mothers’ wombs to drive the pagans out of those holy fields. Over those acres walked the blessed feet that were nailed to the bitter cross fourteen hundred years ago, for our salvation. But this plan of ours is a year old already, and it’s useless to tell you that we will go. That isn’t why we are meeting now. Instead, my noble cousin Westmoreland, tell me what our Council decided last night about advancing this urgent expedition.

WESTMORELAND. My lord, this urgent matter was hotly debated, and many of the duties and costs were drawn up just last night. Then a messenger interrupted us, arriving from Wales with heavy news. The worst of it was that the noble Mortimer had been captured by that crude Welshman. Mortimer was leading the men of Herefordshire against the unruly, savage Glendower when it happened. A thousand of his men were butchered. Then the Welshwomen abused their corpses so savagely and shamelessly, mutilating them like beasts, that it can’t be retold or even mentioned without great shame.
KING. So it seems that news of this fighting broke off our plans for the Holy Land.

WESTMORELAND. Yes, this along with other news, my gracious lord. Even more troubling and unwelcome news came from the North, and this is what it said. On Holy Cross Day, the brave Hotspur, young Harry Percy, met the bold Archibald, that ever-courageous Scot of proven worth, at Holmedon. There they spent a grim and bloody hour. The news was reported from the sound of their cannon fire and from what seemed likely. The man who brought it took to his horse in the very heat and height of the battle, with no idea how it would end.

KING. Here is a dear, truly hard-working friend, Sir Walter Blunt, just now off his horse. He’s spattered with every kind of soil between Holmedon and this palace of ours. And he has brought us pleasant, welcome news. The Earl of Douglas is defeated. Sir Walter saw ten thousand bold Scots and twenty-two knights heaped up in their own blood on Holmedon’s plains. Hotspur took prisoners: Mordake, Earl of Fife and eldest son of the beaten Douglas, and the Earls of Athol, Murray, Angus and Menteith. Isn’t this honorable plunder, a splendid prize? Ha, cousin, isn’t it?
WESTMORELAND. Truly, it’s a victory a prince could boast about.

KING. Yes, and that’s what makes me sad. It makes me commit the sin of envy, that Lord Northumberland should be the father of such a blessed son. His son is the subject everyone speaks of when they speak of honor. He is the straightest tree in the whole grove, Lady Luck’s darling and her pride. Meanwhile, as I watch him praised, I see wild living and disgrace smear the forehead of my young Harry. Oh, if only it could be proved that some fairy, roaming by night, had swapped our children in their cradles! Then mine would be called Percy, and his Plantagenet. I would have his Harry, and he would have mine. But let me put him out of my mind. What do you think, cousin, of young Percy’s arrogance? He is keeping the prisoners he captured in this battle for himself. He sends me word that I’ll get none of them except Mordake, Earl of Fife.
WESTMORELAND. That’s his uncle’s doing. That’s Worcester, who is hostile to you in every way. He makes Hotspur preen himself like a bird and raise his youthful crest against your royal authority.

KING. But I have summoned him to answer for this. And because of it, we must put aside our holy plan to go to Jerusalem for a while. Cousin, next Wednesday we will hold our Council at Windsor; let the lords know. But come back to me yourself quickly. There is more to be said and done than I can express while I’m this angry.
WESTMORELAND. I will, my lord.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — The same. An Apartment of Prince Henry’s
paragraphs: [Prince Henry and Sir John Falstaff enter.]
FALSTAFF. Now, Hal, what time of day is it, lad?

PRINCE. Your wits are so fat from drinking old sherry, unbuttoning your clothes after dinner and sleeping on benches all afternoon that you’ve forgotten how to ask for what you really want to know. What the devil do you care what time of day it is? Hours would have to be cups of sherry, minutes roast chickens, clocks the tongues of pimps, sundials the signs of brothels, and the blessed sun himself a pretty, hot whore in flame-colored silk. Otherwise I see no reason why you would bother to ask the time of day.

FALSTAFF. Actually, you’ve got me there, Hal. We who steal purses go by the moon and the seven stars, not by the sun god Phoebus, that fair wandering knight. And I beg you, sweet joker, when you’re king—God save your Grace—or Your Majesty, I should say, because you’ll have no grace at all—
PRINCE. What, none?
FALSTAFF. No, I swear, not even enough to say grace before a snack of egg and butter.
PRINCE. Well, what then? Come on, get to the point, get to the point.

FALSTAFF. Well then, sweet joker, when you are king, don’t let those of us who serve the night be called thieves who waste the daylight. Let us be called the moon goddess Diana’s foresters, gentlemen of the shadows, darlings of the moon. Let people say we are men of good conduct, because, like the sea, we are governed by our noble, chaste mistress the moon. It is under her face that we steal.

PRINCE. Well said, and the comparison holds up, too. The fortune of us moon’s men ebbs and flows like the sea, since, like the sea, we’re governed by the moon. Here’s the proof. A purse of gold is boldly snatched on Monday night and wildly spent by Tuesday morning. It’s won by yelling “Lay by” and spent by shouting “Bring in.” One moment it’s at low tide, as low as the bottom of the ladder. The next it’s at high tide, as high as the crossbar of the gallows.
FALSTAFF. By God, you’re right, lad. And isn’t the hostess of the tavern a sweet piece of work?
PRINCE. Sweet as honey from Hybla, my old rascal of the castle. And isn’t a sheriff’s leather jacket a nice, long-lasting thing to be locked up in?
FALSTAFF. What’s this, what’s this, you crazy joker? Still at your wisecracks and quibbles? What the plague do I care about a sheriff’s leather jacket?
PRINCE. Well, what the pox do I care about the hostess of the tavern?
FALSTAFF. Well, you’ve called her to settle the bill plenty of times.
PRINCE. Did I ever ask you to pay your share?
FALSTAFF. No, I’ll give you credit, you’ve paid for everything there.
PRINCE. Yes, and elsewhere too, as far as my money would stretch. And where it wouldn’t, I’ve used my credit.

FALSTAFF. Yes, and used it so much that if it weren’t obvious that you are the heir apparent—But please, sweet joker, will there still be gallows standing in England when you are king? Will a man’s courage still be checked, as it is now, by the rusty bridle of that old clown, the law? When you are king, don’t hang a thief.
PRINCE. No, you will.
FALSTAFF. I will? Oh, splendid! By God, I’ll be a fine judge.
PRINCE. You’re judging wrong already. I mean that you’ll be in charge of hanging the thieves, and so you’ll become a splendid hangman.
FALSTAFF. Well, Hal, well. In a way it suits my temperament as well as hanging around at court does, I can tell you.
PRINCE. For getting favors granted?
FALSTAFF. Yes, for getting suits of clothes, and the hangman has no shortage of those in his wardrobe. God’s blood, I’m as gloomy as a neutered tomcat or a bear on a chain.
PRINCE. Or an old lion, or a lover’s lute.
FALSTAFF. Yes, or the drone of a Lincolnshire bagpipe.
PRINCE. What do you say to a hare, or the gloom of the Moor-ditch sewer?

FALSTAFF. You come up with the most tasteless comparisons. You really are the most simile-making, rascally, sweet young prince. But, Hal, please stop bothering me with this nonsense. I wish to God you and I knew where we could buy a supply of good reputations. An old lord of the Council scolded me in the street about you the other day, sir. But I paid no attention to him. And yet he spoke very wisely, but I ignored him. And yet he spoke wisely, and in the street, too.
PRINCE. You did well, for the Bible says wisdom cries out in the streets and no one listens to it.

FALSTAFF. Oh, you have a damnable habit of quoting scripture, and you really could corrupt a saint. You’ve done me a lot of harm, Hal, God forgive you for it. Before I knew you, Hal, I knew nothing bad, and now, to tell the truth, I’m hardly better than one of the wicked. I have to give up this life, and I will give it up. By God, if I don’t, I’m a villain. I won’t be damned for any king’s son in all Christendom.
PRINCE. Where should we steal a purse tomorrow, Jack?
FALSTAFF. God’s wounds, wherever you like, lad, I’ll be one of the gang. If I’m not, call me a villain and disgrace me publicly.
PRINCE. I see you’ve really reformed your life, from praying to purse-snatching.
FALSTAFF. Why, Hal, it’s my calling, Hal. It’s no sin for a man to work at his calling.
[Poins enters.]

Poins!—Now we’ll find out whether Gadshill has set up a robbery. Oh, if men were saved by what they deserved, what hole in hell would be hot enough for him? He’s the most all-powerful villain who ever shouted “Stand!” at an honest man.
PRINCE. Good morning, Ned.

POINS. Good morning, sweet Hal.—What does Monsieur Remorse have to say? What does Sir John Sherry-and-Sugar say? Jack, how are you and the devil getting along about your soul? You sold it to him last Good Friday for a cup of Madeira wine and a cold chicken leg.
PRINCE. Sir John is keeping his word, and the devil will get his bargain. He has never yet broken a proverb, and he will give the devil his due.
POINS. Then you’re damned for keeping your word to the devil.
PRINCE. Otherwise he would be damned for cheating the devil.

POINS. But, my boys, my boys, tomorrow morning, at four o’clock sharp at Gad’s Hill, there will be pilgrims heading to Canterbury with rich offerings, and merchants riding to London with fat purses. I have masks for all of you; you have your own horses. Gadshill is spending tonight in Rochester. I’ve ordered supper for tomorrow night in Eastcheap. We can do it as safely as sleeping. If you’ll come, I’ll stuff your purses full of gold crowns. If you won’t, stay at home and be hanged.
FALSTAFF. Listen, Edward, if I stay at home and don’t go, I’ll hang you for going.
POINS. You will, fatface?
FALSTAFF. Hal, will you be one of us?
PRINCE. Who, me rob? Me, a thief? Not me, I swear.
FALSTAFF. There’s no honesty, manhood or good fellowship in you. You’re not even of royal blood if you don’t dare to fight for ten shillings.
PRINCE. Well then, for once in my life I’ll be a wild man.
FALSTAFF. Why, that’s well said.
PRINCE. Well, whatever happens, I’ll stay home.
FALSTAFF. By God, then I’ll be a traitor when you’re king.
PRINCE. I don’t care.
POINS. Sir John, please leave the Prince and me alone. I’ll give him such good reasons for this adventure that he’ll go.

FALSTAFF. Well, may God give you the gift of persuasion and give him ears that learn. Then what you say may move him, and what he hears may be believed. That way the true prince may, just for fun, turn into a false thief, since the petty crimes of these times need a patron. Goodbye, you’ll find me in Eastcheap.
PRINCE. Goodbye, you late spring! Goodbye, you Indian summer at All Saints’ Day!
[Falstaff exits.]

POINS. Now, my good, sweet, honeyed lord, ride with us tomorrow. I have a joke to play that I can’t pull off alone. Falstaff, Bardolph, Peto and Gadshill will rob those men we’ve already set the trap for. You and I won’t be there. And once they have the loot, if you and I don’t rob them of it, cut this head off my shoulders.
PRINCE. But how will we separate from them when we set out?

POINS. Why, we’ll leave before or after them and arrange a meeting place with them, which we’ll deliberately fail to show up at. Then they’ll go ahead and attempt the robbery themselves. And as soon as they’ve pulled it off, we’ll attack them.
PRINCE. Yes, but they’ll probably recognize us by our horses, by our clothes and by every other piece of our gear.

POINS. Nonsense, they won’t see our horses; I’ll tie them up in the woods. We’ll change our masks after we leave them. And listen, I have coarse linen covers just for the occasion, to hide our recognizable outer clothes.
PRINCE. Yes, but I’m afraid they’ll be too strong for us.

POINS. Well, as for two of them, I know they’re as thoroughbred cowards as ever turned and ran. And as for the third, if he fights any longer than he sees good reason to, I’ll give up carrying weapons. The beauty of this joke will be the outrageous lies this same fat rogue will tell us when we meet at supper. He’ll tell us how he fought at least thirty men, what parries, what blows, what dangers he endured. And exposing those lies is the whole point of the joke.
PRINCE. Well, I’ll go with you. Get everything we need ready and meet me tomorrow night in Eastcheap; I’ll have supper there. Goodbye.
POINS. Goodbye, my lord.
[He exits.]

PRINCE. I know you all, and for a while I will go along with your wild, unrestrained idleness. But in this I will copy the sun. The sun allows low, polluting clouds to smother his beauty and hide it from the world. That way, when he chooses to be himself again, people will marvel at him all the more, since they missed him. He breaks through the foul, ugly mists that seemed to be strangling him. If every day of the year were a holiday, playing would be as boring as working. But because holidays come rarely, people long for them, and nothing pleases like the unusual. So when I throw off this loose behavior and pay a debt I never promised to pay, I’ll prove much better than people expect. And by that much I’ll prove their low expectations wrong. Like bright metal set against a dark background, my reformation will shine out over my faults. It will look finer and attract more attention than goodness that has nothing to contrast with it. I’ll misbehave so cleverly that I make bad behavior a tool. I’ll make up for lost time when people least expect me to.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — The Same. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [King Henry, Northumberland, Worcester, Hotspur, Sir Walter Blunt and others enter.]

KING. My temper has been too cool and calm, too slow to react to these insults. You have noticed this, and so you walk all over my patience. But be sure of this: from now on I will act like what I am, a mighty king who should be feared, rather than follow my natural disposition. My nature has been as smooth as oil and as soft as a baby bird’s feathers. Because of that, it has lost the respect that proud men pay only to the proud.
WORCESTER. Your Majesty, our family hardly deserves to have the whip of royal power used against it. Especially since it is the same power that our own hands helped to make so mighty.
NORTHUMBERLAND. My lord—

KING. Worcester, get out, for I see danger and disobedience in your eye. Oh, sir, your manner is far too bold and arrogant. No king has ever tolerated the defiant frown of a subject. You have my permission to leave us. When we need your help and advice, we’ll send for you.
[Worcester exits.]
[To Northumberland.]
You were about to say something.

NORTHUMBERLAND. Yes, my good lord. Those prisoners Harry Percy here captured at Holmedon, and which were demanded in your Highness’s name, were not refused as forcefully as Your Majesty was told, according to him. So either someone’s malice or a misunderstanding is to blame for this offense, not my son.

HOTSPUR. My lord, I didn’t refuse to hand over any prisoners. But I remember this. When the fighting was over, I was parched with rage and exhaustion, out of breath and faint, leaning on my sword. Then a certain lord came up, neat and smartly dressed, as fresh as a bridegroom. His chin was newly shaved and looked like a field of stubble at harvest time. He was perfumed like a hat-seller. Between his finger and thumb he held a little perfume box, which every now and then he lifted to his nose and took away again. His nose, annoyed, took offense and sniffed each time it came back. And all the while he smiled and chattered. When the soldiers carried dead bodies past, he called them ignorant, ill-mannered louts for bringing a filthy, ugly corpse between the breeze and his noble self. He questioned me in fancy, ladylike holiday language. Among other things, he demanded my prisoners on Your Majesty’s behalf. I was smarting all over, my wounds stiffening as they cooled. Out of pain and impatience at being pestered by such a parrot, I answered carelessly—I don’t know what. He should have them, or he shouldn’t. It drove me mad to see him shine so bright and smell so sweet. He talked like a lady’s maid about guns and drums and wounds, God help us! He told me the best thing on Earth for an internal bruise was whale oil. He said it was a great pity, it really was, that this villainous gunpowder had to be dug out of the bowels of the harmless earth. It had killed many a fine brave fellow in such a cowardly way. If it weren’t for these vile guns, he said, he would have been a soldier himself. My lord, I answered his empty, disjointed chatter offhandedly, as I said. And I beg you, don’t let his report be accepted as an accusation that comes between my love and Your Majesty.

BLUNT. My good lord, consider the circumstances. Whatever Harry Percy said then, to such a person, in such a place, at such a time, together with everything else that’s been reported, could reasonably be allowed to die. It should never rise again to harm him or to count against what he said then, as long as he takes it back now.

KING. But he still refuses to hand over his prisoners, except on one condition and with one exception. He wants us to pay, at our own expense and immediately, the ransom of his brother-in-law, that fool Mortimer. On my soul, Mortimer deliberately betrayed the lives of the men he led to fight against that great magician, that damned Glendower. And we hear that the Earl of March has recently married Glendower’s daughter. Should our treasury be emptied, then, to buy a traitor back home? Should we pay for treason and strike bargains with cowards who have lost and given themselves up? No, let him starve on the barren mountains. I will never count a man my friend whose tongue asks me to spend one penny to ransom the rebel Mortimer.

HOTSPUR. Rebel Mortimer! My sovereign lord, he never deserted you except by the chance of war. To prove that, all it takes is one tongue to speak for all those wounds. Those gaping wounds, like open mouths, he took bravely on the reedy bank of the gentle Severn. There, in single combat, hand to hand, he spent the better part of an hour trading blows with the great Glendower. Three times they stopped for breath. Three times, by agreement, they drank from the swift Severn’s water. The river, frightened by their bloody looks, ran fearfully among the trembling reeds. It hid its curly-waved head under the hollow bank, which was stained with the blood of these brave fighters. Never did mere cheap, rotten scheming disguise itself with such deadly wounds. And the noble Mortimer could never have taken so many, all willingly, as part of a trick. So don’t let him be slandered as a rebel.

KING. You are lying about him, Percy, you are lying about him. He never fought with Glendower. I tell you, he would just as soon have faced the devil alone as take on Owen Glendower as an enemy. Aren’t you ashamed? But, young man, from now on don’t let me hear you speak of Mortimer. Send me your prisoners as quickly as you can, or you’ll hear from me in a way you won’t like.—My Lord Northumberland, you and your son have our permission to leave.—Send us your prisoners, or you’ll hear about it.
[King Henry, Blunt and their attendants exit.]
HOTSPUR. Even if the devil comes and roars for them, I won’t send them. I’ll go after him right now and tell him so. I’ll get it off my chest, even if I risk my head doing it.
NORTHUMBERLAND. What, are you drunk with anger? Stop, and calm down for a moment. Here comes your uncle.
[Worcester enters.]

HOTSPUR. Not speak of Mortimer? God’s wounds, I will speak of him! And let my soul go without mercy if I don’t join him. Yes, for his cause I’ll empty all these veins and shed my precious blood drop by drop in the dust. But I will raise the downtrodden Mortimer as high in the air as this ungrateful King, this thankless, rotten Bolingbroke.
[To Worcester.]
NORTHUMBERLAND. Brother, the King has driven your nephew mad.
WORCESTER. Who stirred up this fury after I left?

HOTSPUR. He wants all my prisoners, if you please! And when I pressed him again about ransoming my wife’s brother, his face went pale. He turned a deadly look on me, trembling at the very name of Mortimer.
WORCESTER. I can’t blame him. Wasn’t Mortimer proclaimed next in line to the throne by Richard, who is now dead?

NORTHUMBERLAND. He was. I heard the proclamation myself. It was at the time when the unfortunate King—may God forgive us the wrongs we did him!—set out on his Irish expedition. He was cut off and came back from there to be deposed, and soon after murdered.
WORCESTER. And for his death the whole world gossips about us, and we live disgraced and badly spoken of.
HOTSPUR. But wait, please. Did King Richard really proclaim my brother-in-law Edmund Mortimer heir to the crown?
NORTHUMBERLAND. He did. I heard it myself.

HOTSPUR. Well, then I can’t blame his cousin the King for wishing he would starve on the barren mountains. But is it going to be said that you two set the crown on the head of this forgetful man? That for his sake you bear the hated stain of having arranged a murder? Is it going to be said that you bring a world of curses down on yourselves? You were his agents, his lowly tools—the ropes, the ladder, or rather the hangman himself. Oh, forgive me for stooping so low to show the rank and position you hold under this cunning King. Shall it be said today, to your shame, or written in history books in time to come, that men of your nobility and power pledged themselves to an unjust cause? Both of you did so, God forgive you. You put down Richard, that sweet lovely rose, and planted this thorn, this cankerworm, Bolingbroke. And shall it be said, to your even greater shame, that you have been fooled, discarded and thrown off by the very man for whom you suffered these disgraces? No. There’s still time to win back your lost honor and restore yourselves to the world’s good opinion. Take revenge on the mocking, scornful contempt of this proud King. Day and night he’s thinking of how to settle the debt he owes you, even if he pays it with your blood and your deaths. So I say—

WORCESTER. Quiet, nephew, say no more. Now I’ll open a secret book. To your discontent, which is quick to understand, I’ll read out matter that is deep and dangerous. It’s as full of peril and daring as walking across a loud, roaring current on the shaky footing of a spear laid over it.

HOTSPUR. If we fall in, good night—sink or swim! Send danger from east to west, as long as honor crosses it from north to south, and let them wrestle it out. Oh, the blood stirs more to rouse a lion than to startle a hare!
NORTHUMBERLAND. Dreaming of some great deed is driving him past the limits of his patience.

HOTSPUR. By heaven, I think it would be an easy leap to snatch bright honor from the pale-faced moon. Or to dive to the bottom of the sea, where no measuring line could ever touch the floor, and pull drowned honor up by the hair. Then whoever rescued her from there could wear all her glories without any rival. But to hell with this half-hearted partnership!
WORCESTER. He imagines a whole world of fancy images here, but not the actual business he ought to pay attention to.—Good nephew, listen to me for a while.
HOTSPUR. I beg your pardon.
WORCESTER. Those same noble Scots who are your prisoners—
HOTSPUR. I’ll keep them all. By God, he won’t have a single Scot of them. No, not if one Scot would save his soul, he won’t. I’ll keep them, I swear by this hand!
WORCESTER. You fly off and won’t listen to what I mean. You shall keep those prisoners—

HOTSPUR. Yes, I will, and that’s final. He said he wouldn’t ransom Mortimer. He forbade me to speak of Mortimer. But I’ll find him when he’s lying asleep and shout “Mortimer!” in his ear. No, I’ll get a starling taught to say nothing but “Mortimer,” and give it to him to keep his anger stirred up forever.
WORCESTER. Listen, nephew, just a word.

HOTSPUR. I solemnly give up every pursuit here except how to annoy and torment this Bolingbroke. And that brawling, sword-and-shield Prince of Wales—if I didn’t think his father doesn’t love him and would be glad if some accident happened to him, I’d have him poisoned with a pot of beer.
WORCESTER. Goodbye, nephew. I’ll talk to you when you’re in a better mood to listen.
NORTHUMBERLAND. What an impatient fool you are, as if a wasp had stung you, to fly into this hysterical mood! You won’t listen to any tongue but your own!

HOTSPUR. Well, look, I feel whipped and beaten with rods, stung by nettles and bitten by ants, when I hear of this vile schemer, Bolingbroke. In Richard’s time—what do you call the place? Damn it! It’s in Gloucestershire. It was where his uncle, the crazy Duke of York, lived. That’s where I first bent my knee to this king of smiles, this Bolingbroke. God’s blood, that was when you and he came back from Ravenspurgh.
NORTHUMBERLAND. At Berkeley Castle.

HOTSPUR. That’s right. Why, what a sugary load of courtesy this fawning greyhound offered me then! “Look, when my infant fortune comes of age,” and “Gentle Harry Percy,” and “kind cousin.” Oh, the devil take such cheats!—God forgive me! Good uncle, tell your story. I’m finished.
WORCESTER. No, if you’re not, go at it again. We’ll wait until you’re ready.
HOTSPUR. I’m finished, honestly.

WORCESTER. Then back once more to your Scottish prisoners. Release them right away without ransom. Make Douglas’s son your only means of raising forces in Scotland. Rest assured, that will be easily granted, for various reasons I’ll send you in writing.—[To Northumberland.] You, my lord, while your son is busy in Scotland this way, must secretly worm your way into the confidence of that noble and well-loved churchman, the Archbishop.
HOTSPUR. Of York, isn’t it?

WORCESTER. Yes. He resents his brother Lord Scroop’s death at Bristol. I’m not saying this as a guess, as something I think might happen. I’m saying what I know has been considered, plotted and set down. It’s only waiting to see the right opportunity to bring it on.
HOTSPUR. I can smell it. Upon my life, it will go well.
NORTHUMBERLAND. You always let the hounds loose before the game is even started.
HOTSPUR. Why, it can’t help but be a noble plot. And then the forces of Scotland and of York will join with Mortimer, right?
WORCESTER. And so they will.
HOTSPUR. Honestly, it’s extremely well aimed.

WORCESTER. And there’s no small reason pushing us to hurry. We must save our heads by raising an army. However evenly we behave, the King will always think he’s in our debt. He’ll think we consider ourselves unrewarded, until he finds a time to pay us back in full. And look how he’s already starting to withhold his loving looks from us, as if we were strangers.
HOTSPUR. He is, he is. We’ll get our revenge on him.

WORCESTER. Nephew, goodbye. Don’t go any further in this than I direct you in my letters. When the time is ripe, which will be soon, I’ll slip away to Glendower and Lord Mortimer. There you and Douglas and all our forces will meet at once, as I’ll arrange it. Then we’ll hold our fortunes in our own strong arms, when right now they are very uncertain.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Goodbye, good brother. We’ll succeed, I trust.
HOTSPUR. Uncle, goodbye. Oh, let the hours pass quickly until battlefields and blows and groans applaud our game!
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Rochester. An Inn-Yard
paragraphs: [A Carrier enters with a lantern in his hand.]
FIRST CARRIER. Heigh-ho! If it isn’t four in the morning, I’ll be hanged. The Big Dipper is over the new chimney, and our horse still isn’t loaded.—Hey, stable boy!
OSTLER. [From offstage.] Coming, coming.
FIRST CARRIER. Please, Tom, beat the dust out of Cut’s saddle and stuff some wool into the front of it. The poor nag is rubbed raw on the shoulders beyond all measure.
[Another Carrier enters.]
SECOND CARRIER. The peas and beans here are as damp as a dog, and that’s the quickest way to give poor horses worms. This inn has been turned upside down since Robin the stable boy died.
FIRST CARRIER. The poor fellow was never happy after the price of oats went up. It was the death of him.
SECOND CARRIER. I think this is the worst inn on the whole London road for fleas. I’m as spotted with bites as a tench fish.
FIRST CARRIER. Like a tench! By the Mass, no Christian king could have been bitten worse than I have been since the first rooster crowed.
SECOND CARRIER. Well, they won’t give us a single chamber pot, so we pee in the fireplace. And urine breeds fleas like a loach breeds little fish.
FIRST CARRIER. Hey, stable boy! Come out here and be hanged, come on.
SECOND CARRIER. I have a side of bacon and two roots of ginger to be delivered all the way to Charing Cross.

FIRST CARRIER. God’s body! The turkeys in my basket are starving to death.—Hey, stable boy! A plague on you! Don’t you have eyes in your head? Can’t you hear? If cracking your skull wouldn’t be as good a deed as having a drink, I’m a real villain. Come here and be hanged. Don’t you have any honesty in you?
[Gadshill enters.]
GADSHILL. Good morning, carriers. What time is it?
FIRST CARRIER. I think it’s two o’clock.
GADSHILL. Please, lend me your lantern so I can see my horse in the stable.
FIRST CARRIER. No, by God, hold on! I know a trick worth two of that, honestly.
GADSHILL. Please, lend me yours.
SECOND CARRIER. Oh, sure, when? Can you tell me? “Lend me your lantern,” he says! Indeed, I’ll see you hanged first.
GADSHILL. Carrier, what time do you plan to get to London?

SECOND CARRIER. Early enough to go to bed by candlelight, I promise you. Come on, neighbor Mugs, let’s wake up the gentlemen. They want to travel in company, because they’re carrying a lot of valuables.
[The Carriers exit.]
GADSHILL. Hey there! Chamberlain!
[The Chamberlain enters.]
CHAMBERLAIN. Right here, as the pickpocket said.

GADSHILL. That’s just as good as saying “right here, as the chamberlain said,” because you differ from a pickpocket no more than giving directions differs from doing the work. You’re the one who plans how it’s done.

CHAMBERLAIN. Good morning, Master Gadshill. What I told you last night still holds. There’s a wealthy farmer from the Weald of Kent who has brought three hundred marks in gold with him. I heard him tell one of his companions at supper last night. That one is a sort of accountant, who also has plenty of valuables with him, God knows what. They’re already up and calling for eggs and butter. They’ll be leaving soon.
GADSHILL. Listen, if they don’t meet any highwaymen on the road, I’ll give you my neck.
CHAMBERLAIN. No, I don’t want it. Please save that for the hangman. I know you worship Saint Nicholas, the patron of thieves, as faithfully as any dishonest man can.

GADSHILL. Why are you talking to me about the hangman? If I hang, I’ll make a fat pair of gallows. Because if I hang, old Sir John hangs with me, and you know he’s no skinny weakling. Come on, there are other heroes you don’t dream of. For the fun of it, they’re happy to do our trade some honor. If anyone looked into things, they would fix everything for the sake of their own reputations. I’m not joined up with any common foot-robbers or cudgel-swinging sixpenny thugs. I don’t run with those crazy, mustached, purple-faced beer-swillers. I’m in with nobility and easygoing gentlemen, mayors and great ones. They’re the kind who can keep a secret, who would rather strike than talk, and talk rather than drink, and drink rather than pray. And yet, damn it, I’m lying, because they pray constantly to their saint, the commonwealth. Or rather they don’t pray to her, they prey on her. They ride up and down on her and use her for their boots.
CHAMBERLAIN. What, use the commonwealth as their boots? Will she keep the water out on a muddy road?

GADSHILL. She will, she will. Justice has greased her to waterproof her. We steal as safely as if we were in a castle, totally sure of ourselves. We have the recipe of fern seed, so we walk invisible.
CHAMBERLAIN. No, honestly, I think you owe more to the dark of night than to fern seed for walking around invisible.
GADSHILL. Shake my hand. You’ll have a share of our loot, as sure as I’m an honest man.
CHAMBERLAIN. No, I’d rather have it as sure as you’re a lying thief.
GADSHILL. Come on. The word for man is a name common to all men, honest or not. Tell the stable boy to bring my horse out of the stable. Goodbye, you dirty rascal.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — The Road by Gads-hill
paragraphs: [Prince Henry and Poins enter; Bardolph and Peto follow some distance behind.]
POINS. Come on, hide, hide! I’ve taken Falstaff’s horse away, and he’s fretting like stiffened cheap velvet.
PRINCE. Stay hidden.
[They step aside.]
[Falstaff enters.]
FALSTAFF. Poins! Poins, and go hang yourself! Poins!
[The Prince comes forward.]
PRINCE. Quiet, you fat-kidneyed rascal! What a racket you’re making!
FALSTAFF. Where’s Poins, Hal?
PRINCE. He’s walked up to the top of the hill. I’ll go look for him.
[He steps back out of sight.]

FALSTAFF. I’m cursed to be robbing in that thief’s company. The rascal has moved my horse and tied him up who knows where. If I walk even four more feet by the measuring rule, I’ll run out of breath. Well, I fully expect to die a decent death in spite of all this, as long as I escape hanging for killing that rogue. I’ve sworn off his company every hour of every day for twenty-two years, and yet I’m bewitched by the rogue’s company. If the rascal hasn’t given me love potions to make me love him, I’ll be hanged. It can’t be anything else: I’ve drunk potions. Poins! Hal! A plague on you both! Bardolph! Peto! I’ll starve before I rob one more foot of the way. If it wouldn’t be as good a deed as drinking to turn honest and leave these rogues, then I’m the lowest scoundrel who ever chewed with a tooth. Eight yards of uneven ground is seventy miles to me on foot, and these stony-hearted villains know it perfectly well. A plague on it, when thieves can’t be loyal to each other! [They whistle.] Whew! A plague on all of you! Give me my horse, you rogues, give me my horse and go hang!
PRINCE. [Coming forward.] Quiet, you fat guts! Lie down, put your ear close to the ground, and listen whether you can hear the footsteps of travelers.

FALSTAFF. Have you got any crowbars to lift me up again once I’m down? By God’s blood, I won’t carry my own flesh so far on foot again for all the money in your father’s treasury. What the plague do you mean by tricking me like this?
PRINCE. You’re lying. You’re not colted, meaning tricked. You’re uncolted, meaning without a horse.
FALSTAFF. Please, good Prince Hal, help me get to my horse, good king’s son.
PRINCE. Get away, you rogue! Am I supposed to be your stable boy?

FALSTAFF. Go hang yourself with your own crown-prince garters! If I get caught, I’ll turn informer on all of you for this. If I don’t have ballads written about you all and sung to dirty tunes, let a cup of sherry be my poison. A joke going this far, and on foot too! I hate it.
[Gadshill enters.]
GADSHILL. Stand still!
FALSTAFF. I’m standing, all right, against my will.
POINS. Oh, it’s our scout who set up the job. I know his voice.
[Poins comes forward with Bardolph and Peto.]
BARDOLPH. What’s the news?
GADSHILL. Cover up, cover up, put on your masks. There’s the King’s money coming down the hill. It’s on its way to the King’s treasury.
FALSTAFF. You’re lying, you rogue. It’s on its way to the King’s tavern.
GADSHILL. There’s enough to make us all rich.
FALSTAFF. Enough to get us all hanged.
PRINCE. Gentlemen, you four will face them in the narrow lane. Ned Poins and I will wait farther down. If they escape from you, they’ll run right into us.
PETO. How many of them are there?
GADSHILL. Around eight or ten.
FALSTAFF. God’s wounds! Won’t they rob us instead?
PRINCE. What, are you a coward, Sir John Potbelly?
FALSTAFF. It’s true, I’m not as lean as John of Gaunt, your grandfather, but I’m still no coward, Hal.
PRINCE. Well, we’ll leave that to be proved.
POINS. Jack, your horse is behind the hedge. When you need him, that’s where you’ll find him. Goodbye, and stand firm.
FALSTAFF. I couldn’t hit him now even if I were going to be hanged for not doing it.
PRINCE. [Aside to Poins.] Ned, where are our disguises?
POINS. [Aside to Prince Henry.] Right here, close by. Stay hidden.
[The Prince and Poins exit.]
FALSTAFF. Now, gentlemen, good luck to every man, I say. Everyone to his job.
[The Travelers enter.]
FIRST TRAVELLER. Come on, neighbor, the boy will lead our horses down the hill. We’ll walk on foot for a while and stretch our legs.
THIEVES. Stand still!
SECOND TRAVELLER. Jesus bless us!
FALSTAFF. Hit them, knock them down, cut the villains’ throats! Ah, you bastard caterpillars, you bacon-fed scum, they hate us young people. Down with them, fleece them!
FIRST TRAVELLER. Oh, we’re ruined, both we and our families forever!

FALSTAFF. Go hang, you potbellied scum, are you ruined? No, you fat misers, I wish all your wealth were here! Move it, you slabs of bacon, move! What, you scum! Young men have to live. You’re respectable jurymen, are you? We’ll jury you, by God.
[They rob the travelers and tie them up. They all exit.]
[Prince Henry and Poins enter, disguised in coarse linen suits.]

PRINCE. The thieves have tied up the honest men. Now, if you and I could rob the thieves and ride happily to London, it would be something to talk about for a week, laugh about for a month, and a good joke forever.
POINS. Stay hidden. I hear them coming.
[They step back out of sight.]
[The Thieves enter again.]

FALSTAFF. Come on, gentlemen, let’s split it, and then get on our horses before daylight. If the Prince and Poins aren’t two complete cowards, there’s no justice left in the world. There’s no more courage in that Poins than in a wild duck.
[While they are dividing the money, the Prince and Poins attack them.]
PRINCE. Your money!
POINS. Villains!
[After a blow or two, Falstaff and the others run away, leaving the loot behind them.]

PRINCE. That was easily won. Now let’s get on our horses and go merrily. The thieves are all scattered, and so full of fear that they don’t dare come near each other. Each one thinks his partner is a constable. Let’s go, good Ned. Falstaff is sweating himself to death, and he greases the lean earth with his fat as he walks along. If I weren’t laughing, I’d feel sorry for him.
POINS. How the fat rogue bellowed!
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — Warkworth. A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Hotspur enters, reading a letter.]

HOTSPUR. “But for my own part, my lord, I would be quite happy to be there, because of the love I have for your family.” He would be happy to be there, so why isn’t he? Because of the love he has for our house! What he shows here is that he loves his own barn more than he loves our house. Let me read some more. “The plan you are undertaking is dangerous.” Well, of course it is. It’s dangerous to catch a cold, to sleep, to drink. But I tell you, my lord fool, out of this nettle, danger, we pick this flower, safety. “The plan you are undertaking is dangerous, the allies you have named are unreliable, the timing is badly chosen, and your whole plot is too weak to balance against so great an opposition.” Is that what you say? Is that so? I say back to you, you are a shallow, cowardly peasant, and you lie. What a brainless idiot this is! By the Lord, our plot is as good a plot as was ever made. Our friends are true and loyal. It’s a good plot, with good friends, and full of promise. It’s an excellent plot, with very good friends. What a cold-blooded rogue this is! Why, my Lord of York approves the plot and the whole plan of action. God’s wounds, if I were next to this rascal now, I could knock his brains out with his lady’s fan. Aren’t my father, my uncle and I in it? And Lord Edmund Mortimer, my Lord of York, and Owen Glendower? Isn’t the Douglas in it besides? Don’t I have letters from all of them, promising to meet me armed by the ninth of next month? And haven’t some of them already set out? What a heathen rascal this is, an unbeliever! Ha! Just watch, now. Out of pure fear and a cold heart, he’ll go to the King and reveal everything we’re doing. Oh, I could split myself in two and beat myself up, for asking such a bowl of skim milk to join so honorable an undertaking! Hang him, let him tell the King. We are ready. I’ll set out tonight.
[Lady Percy enters.]
Well, Kate! I have to leave you within two hours.

LADY PERCY. Oh, my good lord, why are you always alone like this? What have I done wrong that I’ve been banished from my Harry’s bed for two weeks? Tell me, sweet lord, what is it that has taken away your appetite, your pleasure and your golden sleep? Why do you keep your eyes fixed on the ground, and jump so often when you sit alone? Why have you lost the fresh color in your cheeks? Why have you handed over my treasures and my rights in you to dull-eyed brooding and cursed gloom? I’ve kept watch beside you in your restless sleep. I’ve heard you mutter stories of iron wars and call out riding commands to your leaping horse. You’ve cried “Courage! To the battlefield!” And you’ve talked of attacks and retreats, of trenches and tents, of stake fences, forts and parapets. You’ve talked of great cannons, small cannons and long guns, of ransoms for prisoners and of soldiers killed, and all the twists and turns of a furious battle. Your spirit inside you has been so at war, and has stirred you up so much in your sleep, that beads of sweat have stood on your forehead like bubbles in a stream just disturbed. And strange expressions have appeared on your face, like the ones we see when men hold their breath at some great and sudden command. Oh, what do these signs mean? My lord has some serious business on hand, and I must know it, or else he doesn’t love me.
HOTSPUR. Hey, there!
[A Servant enters.]
Has Gilliams left with the package?
SERVANT. He has, my lord, an hour ago.
HOTSPUR. Has Butler brought those horses from the sheriff?
SERVANT. He brought one horse, my lord, just now.
HOTSPUR. Which horse? A roan with clipped ears, isn’t it?
SERVANT. It is, my lord.
HOTSPUR. That roan will be my throne. Well, I’ll ride him right away. Oh, Esperance, the Percy battle cry! Tell Butler to lead him out into the park.
[The Servant exits.]
LADY PERCY. But listen to me, my lord.
HOTSPUR. What are you saying, my lady?
LADY PERCY. What is it that’s carrying you away?
HOTSPUR. Why, my horse, my love, my horse.

LADY PERCY. Come off it, you crazy-headed ape! A weasel doesn’t have half as much bad temper as you’re tossed about with. I swear, I’ll find out your business, Harry, I really will. I’m afraid my brother Mortimer is making a move about his claim to the crown, and has sent for you to back up his enterprise. But if you go—
HOTSPUR. If I go that far on foot, I’ll be tired, love.
LADY PERCY. Come on, come on, you parrot, answer the question I’m asking you, straight. I swear, I’ll break your little finger, Harry, if you won’t tell me everything truthfully.

HOTSPUR. Go away, go away, you time-waster! Love? I don’t love you. I don’t care about you, Kate. This is no world for playing with dolls and jousting with lips. We need bloody noses and cracked heads, and we have to pass them around like coins too. God save me, my horse! What are you saying, Kate? What do you want from me?
LADY PERCY. Don’t you love me? Don’t you really? Well, don’t, then. Since you don’t love me, I won’t love myself. Don’t you love me? No, tell me whether you’re joking or not.

HOTSPUR. Come on, do you want to watch me ride? And once I’m on horseback, I’ll swear I love you infinitely. But listen, Kate. From now on you mustn’t ask me where I’m going, or argue about why. Where I have to go, I have to go. And to sum up, I must leave you this evening, gentle Kate. I know you’re wise, but no wiser than Harry Percy’s wife should be. You’re loyal, but you’re still a woman. And as for keeping secrets, no lady keeps them better, because I’m quite sure you won’t reveal what you don’t know. That’s how far I’ll trust you, gentle Kate.
LADY PERCY. What? Only that far?
HOTSPUR. Not an inch further. But listen, Kate. Wherever I go, you’ll go there too. I’ll set out today, and you tomorrow. Will that satisfy you, Kate?
LADY PERCY. It will have to.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — Eastcheap. A Room in the Boar’s Head Tavern
paragraphs: [Prince Henry enters.]
PRINCE. Ned, please come out of that stuffy room and help me laugh a little.
[Poins enters.]
POINS. Where have you been, Hal?

PRINCE. With three or four blockheads among sixty or eighty barrels of wine. I’ve hit the lowest note of humility. Listen, I’m now sworn brother to a trio of waiters, and I can call them all by their first names, Tom, Dick and Francis. They already swear on their souls that though I’m only the Prince of Wales, I’m the king of courtesy. They tell me flat out that I’m no stuck-up jerk like Falstaff, but a real sport, a lad with guts, a good boy. By the Lord, that’s what they call me! And when I’m King of England, I’ll command all the good lads in Eastcheap. They call drinking deep “dyeing scarlet.” And when you stop for a breath in mid-gulp, they shout “Hem!” and tell you to “Play it off!” In short, in a quarter of an hour I’ve learned so well that I can drink with any tinker in his own lingo for the rest of my life. I tell you, Ned, you’ve lost a lot of honor by not being with me in this campaign. But, sweet Ned, to sweeten that name of Ned, I’ll give you this pennyworth of sugar. An assistant bartender slapped it into my hand just now. He’s a fellow who never spoke any English in his life except “Eight shillings and sixpence,” and “You are welcome.” He adds a shrill cry: “Coming, coming, sir! Charge a pint of sweet wine to the Half-Moon room,” or something like that. But, Ned, to pass the time until Falstaff gets here, please stand in some side room. I’ll ask my puny waiter why he gave me the sugar. You keep calling “Francis” the whole time, so that all he can ever say to me is “Coming.” Step aside, and I’ll show you an example.
[Poins exits.]
POINS. [Offstage.] Francis!
PRINCE. You’re perfect.
POINS. [Offstage.] Francis!
[Francis enters.]
FRANCIS. Coming, coming, sir. Go check on the Pomegranate room, Ralph.
PRINCE. Come here, Francis.
FRANCIS. My lord?
PRINCE. How long do you still have to serve as an apprentice, Francis?
FRANCIS. Truly, five years, and as much as—
POINS. [Offstage.] Francis!
FRANCIS. Coming, coming, sir.

PRINCE. Five years! By Our Lady, that’s a long contract for clinking pewter mugs! But, Francis, would you dare to be brave enough to play the coward with your apprenticeship contract, show it a good pair of heels, and run away from it?
FRANCIS. Oh Lord, sir, I’d swear on every Bible in England that in my heart I could—
POINS. [Offstage.] Francis!
FRANCIS. Coming, sir.
PRINCE. How old are you, Francis?
FRANCIS. Let me see, by next Michaelmas I’ll be—
POINS. [Offstage.] Francis!
FRANCIS. Coming, sir. Please wait a moment, my lord.
PRINCE. No, but listen, Francis. About the sugar you gave me, it was a pennyworth, wasn’t it?
FRANCIS. Oh Lord, I wish it had been two!
PRINCE. I’ll give you a thousand pounds for it. Ask me for it whenever you like, and you’ll have it.
POINS. [Offstage.] Francis!
FRANCIS. Coming, coming.
PRINCE. Coming, Francis? No, Francis, but tomorrow, Francis. Or, Francis, on Thursday. Or really, Francis, whenever you like. But, Francis—
FRANCIS. My lord?
PRINCE. Will you rob this leather-jacketed, crystal-buttoned, crew-cut, agate-ringed, dark-wool-stockinged, cheap-tape-gartered, smooth-talking, Spanish-purse-carrying—
FRANCIS. Oh Lord, sir, who do you mean?
PRINCE. Why, then, cheap brown sweet wine is the only drink for you. Because look, Francis, your white canvas jacket will get dirty. In Barbary, sir, it can’t come to that much.
FRANCIS. What, sir?
POINS. [Offstage.] Francis!
PRINCE. Go on, you rogue! Don’t you hear them calling?
[They both call him at once. The waiter stands confused, not knowing which way to go.]
[The Vintner enters.]
VINTNER. What, are you standing still while you hear calling like that? Go take care of the guests inside.
[Francis exits.]
My lord, old Sir John and half a dozen others are at the door. Shall I let them in?
PRINCE. Leave them there for a while, and then open the door.
[The Vintner exits.]
Poins!
[Poins enters.]
POINS. Coming, coming, sir.
PRINCE. Listen, Falstaff and the rest of the thieves are at the door. Shall we have some fun?
POINS. As merry as crickets, my lad. But tell me, what clever game were you playing with this joke on the waiter? Come on, what was the point?
PRINCE. Right now I’m in every mood that has ever shown itself as a mood, from the old days of good old Adam to the young hour of this present midnight.
[Francis enters.]
What time is it, Francis?
FRANCIS. Coming, coming, sir.
[Francis exits.]

PRINCE. To think that this fellow has fewer words than a parrot, and yet he’s the son of a woman! His whole work is going upstairs and downstairs, and his whole eloquence is adding up a bill. I’m not yet in the mood of Percy, the Hotspur of the north. He’s the one who kills some six or seven dozen Scots before breakfast, washes his hands, and says to his wife, “Damn this quiet life! I want work.” “Oh, my sweet Harry,” she says, “how many have you killed today?” “Give my roan horse some medicine,” he says. An hour later he answers, “Some fourteen.” Then he adds, “A trifle, a trifle.” Please, call in Falstaff. I’ll play Percy, and that damned slab of pork will play Dame Mortimer, his wife. Drink up, as the drunkard says. Call in Ribs, call in Tallow.
[Falstaff, Gadshill, Bardolph and Peto enter, followed by Francis with wine.]
POINS. Welcome, Jack. Where have you been?

FALSTAFF. A plague on all cowards, I say, and vengeance too! Indeed, and amen! Give me a cup of sherry, boy. Before I live this life much longer, I’ll take up sewing stockings, and mend them and re-foot them too. A plague on all cowards! Give me a cup of sherry, you rogue. Is there no virtue left in the world?
[He drinks.]
PRINCE. Have you ever seen the sun god (soft-hearted sun god!) kiss a dish of butter, and the butter melt at the sun’s sweet talk? If you have, then look at that mixture there.

FALSTAFF. You scoundrel, there’s lime in this wine too. There’s nothing to be found in wicked mankind but crookedness. Still, a coward is worse than a cup of wine with lime in it. A rotten coward! Go your own way, old Jack. Die whenever you like. If manhood, real manhood, hasn’t vanished from the face of the Earth, then I’m a spawned-out herring. There aren’t three good men left in England who haven’t been hanged, and one of them is fat and getting old, God help us. It’s a bad world, I tell you. I wish I were a weaver; then I could sing psalms or anything else. A plague on all cowards, I still say.
PRINCE. Well, you sack of wool, what are you muttering about?

FALSTAFF. A king’s son! If I don’t beat you out of your kingdom with a wooden toy dagger and drive all your subjects ahead of you like a flock of wild geese, I’ll never grow a beard again. You, the Prince of Wales!
PRINCE. Why, you round son of a whore, what’s the matter?
FALSTAFF. Aren’t you a coward? Answer me that—and Poins there too?
POINS. God’s wounds, you fat belly, if you call me a coward, by the Lord, I’ll stab you.

FALSTAFF. Me, call you a coward? I’ll see you damned before I call you a coward. But I’d give a thousand pounds to run as fast as you can. Your shoulders are straight enough, so you don’t care who sees your back. Do you call that backing up your friends? A plague on that kind of backing! Give me men who will face me.—Give me a cup of wine. I’m a scoundrel if I’ve had a drink today.
PRINCE. Oh, you villain! Your lips have barely been wiped since your last drink.
FALSTAFF. That makes no difference. A plague on all cowards, I still say.
[He drinks.]
PRINCE. What’s the matter?
FALSTAFF. What’s the matter? There are four of us here who took a thousand pounds this very morning.
PRINCE. Where is it, Jack, where is it?
FALSTAFF. Where is it? It was taken from us: a hundred men against just the poor four of us.
PRINCE. What, a hundred, man?

FALSTAFF. I’m a scoundrel if I didn’t fight a dozen of them at close quarters for two hours straight. I escaped by a miracle. My jacket has been stabbed through eight times, my breeches four times. My shield is cut through and through, and my sword is hacked like a handsaw. Look, here’s the proof! I never fought better since I became a man, but it was no use. A plague on all cowards! Let these men tell it. If they say more or less than the truth, they are villains and sons of darkness.
PRINCE. Speak up, gentlemen. How did it happen?
GADSHILL. The four of us attacked about a dozen.
FALSTAFF. Sixteen at least, my lord.
GADSHILL. And we tied them up.
PETO. No, no, they weren’t tied up.
FALSTAFF. You scoundrel, they were tied up, every last one of them, or else I’m a Jew, a Hebrew Jew.
GADSHILL. While we were dividing the money, six or seven fresh men attacked us.
FALSTAFF. And they untied the others, and then the rest of them came at us.
PRINCE. What, you fought with all of them?

FALSTAFF. All? I don’t know what you call all. But if I didn’t fight fifty of them, I’m a bunch of radishes. If there weren’t fifty-two or fifty-three of them on poor old Jack, then I’m not a two-legged creature.
PRINCE. I pray to God you haven’t murdered some of them.

FALSTAFF. No, it’s too late for praying about that. I’ve peppered two of them. Two I’m sure I’ve paid off for good, two scoundrels in canvas suits. I’ll tell you what, Hal: if I’m lying to you, spit in my face and call me a horse. You know my old fighting stance. Here I stood, and this is how I held my sword. Four scoundrels in canvas came charging at me.
PRINCE. What, four? You just said two.
FALSTAFF. Four, Hal. I told you four.
POINS. Yes, yes, he said four.
FALSTAFF. These four came at me head-on and thrust at me with all their strength. I didn’t make any more fuss about it. I just caught all seven of their sword points on my shield, like this.
PRINCE. Seven? Why, there were only four a moment ago.
FALSTAFF. In canvas?
POINS. Yes, four, in canvas suits.
FALSTAFF. Seven, I swear by this sword hilt, or else I’m a villain.
PRINCE. [Aside to Poins.] Please, leave him alone. We’ll get more of this soon.
FALSTAFF. Are you listening to me, Hal?
PRINCE. Yes, and paying close attention too, Jack.
FALSTAFF. Do that, because it’s worth listening to. These nine in canvas that I told you about—
PRINCE. Look, two more already.
FALSTAFF. Their sword points being broken—
POINS. And their other points, the laces holding up their pants, broke too, so their pants fell down.
FALSTAFF. They started to back away from me. But I followed them closely, came at them hand and foot, and quick as a thought I finished off seven of the eleven.
PRINCE. That’s monstrous! Eleven canvas men grown out of two!
FALSTAFF. But as the devil would have it, three bastard scoundrels dressed in Kendal green came up behind me and charged at me. It was so dark, Hal, that you couldn’t see your own hand.

PRINCE. These lies are just like the father who makes them: huge as a mountain, obvious, plain to touch. Why, you clay-brained gut-bag, you knot-headed fool, you son of a whore, you disgusting greasy lump of candle fat—
FALSTAFF. What, are you crazy? Are you crazy? Isn’t the truth the truth?
PRINCE. Why, how could you tell these men were in Kendal green, when it was so dark you couldn’t see your hand? Come on, give us your reason. What do you say to that?
POINS. Come on, your reason, Jack, your reason.

FALSTAFF. What, because I’m forced to? God’s wounds, if I were hung up by the arms in torture, or stretched on every rack in the world, I wouldn’t tell you because I was forced to. Give you a reason under force! Even if reasons were as common as blackberries, I wouldn’t give any man a reason under force, not me.
PRINCE. I won’t be guilty of this sin any longer. This red-faced coward, this bed-squasher, this horse-back-breaker, this huge hill of flesh—

FALSTAFF. God’s blood, you starved runt, you eel-skin, you dried ox tongue, you bull’s penis, you dried codfish—oh, if only I had the breath to say what you’re like! You tailor’s yardstick, you knife sheath, you bow case, you nasty upright skewer of a sword—
PRINCE. Well, catch your breath for a while, and then go at it again. And when you’ve worn yourself out with your low comparisons, just hear me say this.
POINS. Listen, Jack.

PRINCE. The two of us saw you four attack four men. You tied them up and took their money. Now watch how a simple story will bring you down. Then the two of us attacked you four, and with one word we scared you off your loot. We have it, yes, and we can show it to you here in this tavern. And Falstaff, you carried your gut away as nimbly and quickly as anything. You roared for mercy, and kept running and roaring, like any bull-calf I ever heard. What a wretch you are, to hack up your own sword like that and then say it happened in a fight! What trick, what scheme, what rabbit hole can you find now to hide yourself from this open and obvious shame?
POINS. Come on, let’s hear it, Jack. What trick have you got now?

FALSTAFF. By the Lord, I knew it was you as well as the God who made you did. Why, listen, gentlemen: was it my place to kill the heir to the throne? Should I turn on the true prince? Why, you know I’m as brave as Hercules. But think about instinct. The lion won’t touch a true prince. Instinct is a powerful thing. I was a coward on instinct. I’ll think better of myself and of you for the rest of my life—of me as a brave lion, and of you as a true prince. But, by the Lord, boys, I’m glad you have the money.—Hostess, shut the doors. We’ll party tonight and pray tomorrow. Gallants, lads, boys, hearts of gold, may every name of good fellowship be yours! What, shall we have fun? Shall we put on a play on the spot?
PRINCE. Agreed, and the plot will be you running away.
FALSTAFF. Ah, no more of that, Hal, if you love me!
[The Hostess enters.]
HOSTESS. Oh Jesus, my lord the Prince—
PRINCE. Well now, my lady the hostess! What do you have to say to me?
HOSTESS. Indeed, my lord, there’s a nobleman from the court at the door who wants to speak with you. He says he comes from your father.
PRINCE. Give him enough to make him a royal man, and send him back to my mother.
FALSTAFF. What kind of man is he?
HOSTESS. An old man.
FALSTAFF. What is solemn old age doing out of bed at midnight? Shall I give him his answer?
PRINCE. Please do, Jack.
FALSTAFF. Believe me, I’ll send him packing.
[He exits.]
PRINCE. Now, gentlemen, by Our Lady, you fought well. So did you, Peto. So did you, Bardolph. You’re lions too: you ran away on instinct. You won’t touch the true prince—no, shame on you!
BARDOLPH. Honestly, I ran when I saw the others run.
PRINCE. Honestly, tell me now in all seriousness: how did Falstaff’s sword get so hacked up?
PETO. Why, he hacked it with his dagger. He said he would swear the truth right out of England before he’d fail to make you believe it happened in a fight. And he talked us into doing the same.

BARDOLPH. Yes, and he told us to tickle our noses with spear grass to make them bleed. Then we were to smear our clothes with the blood and swear it was the blood of honest men. I did something I hadn’t done in seven years: I blushed to hear his outrageous schemes.

PRINCE. Oh, you villain, you stole a cup of wine eighteen years ago and were caught red-handed. Ever since then you’ve blushed on the spot. You had fire and sword on your side, and still you ran away. What instinct made you do that?
BARDOLPH. My lord, do you see these meteors? Do you see these fiery vapors?
PRINCE. I do.
BARDOLPH. What do you think they predict?
PRINCE. Hot livers and empty wallets.
BARDOLPH. A fiery temper, my lord, if you take it correctly.
PRINCE. No, if you’re taken correctly, a hangman’s noose.
[Falstaff enters.]
Here comes skinny Jack, here comes the bag of bones. How are you, my sweet creature of stuffing? How long has it been, Jack, since you saw your own knee?

FALSTAFF. My own knee? When I was about your age, Hal, my waist was no thicker than an eagle’s claw. I could have crawled through any alderman’s thumb ring. A plague on sighing and grief! It blows a man up like a balloon. There’s terrible news going around. Sir John Bracy was here from your father, and you have to go to court in the morning. That same madman from the north, Percy, is in it. So is the man from Wales who beat the demon Amamon with a stick, gave Lucifer horns, and made the devil swear loyalty to him on the cross of a Welsh pike. What the hell is his name?
POINS. Oh, Glendower.
FALSTAFF. Owen, Owen, that’s the one. And his son-in-law Mortimer, and old Northumberland, and that lively Scot of all Scots, Douglas, who can ride a horse straight up a vertical hill—
PRINCE. The one who rides at full gallop and kills a flying sparrow with his pistol.
FALSTAFF. You’ve hit it.
PRINCE. That’s more than he ever did to the sparrow.
FALSTAFF. Well, that rascal has good mettle in him. He won’t run.
PRINCE. Why, what a rascal you are, then, to praise him for running!
FALSTAFF. On horseback, you cuckoo! But on foot he won’t budge an inch.
PRINCE. Yes, Jack, on instinct.

FALSTAFF. I grant you, on instinct. Well, he’s in it too, and someone named Mordake, and a thousand more blue-capped Scots. Worcester slipped away tonight. Your father’s beard has turned white at the news. You can buy land now as cheap as stinking mackerel.
PRINCE. Why then, if we get a hot June and this civil fighting keeps up, we’ll probably buy virgins the way people buy hobnails, by the hundreds.

FALSTAFF. By the Mass, lad, you’re right. It looks like we’ll have good business that way. But tell me, Hal, aren’t you horribly scared? You’re the heir to the throne. Could the world find you three enemies like that again, that fiend Douglas, that spirit Percy, and that devil Glendower? Aren’t you horribly afraid? Doesn’t your blood shiver at it?
PRINCE. Not one bit, honestly. I lack some of your instinct.
FALSTAFF. Well, you’re going to get scolded horribly tomorrow when you go to your father. If you love me, rehearse an answer.
PRINCE. You play my father and question me about the details of my life.
FALSTAFF. Shall I? Agreed! This chair will be my throne, this dagger my scepter, and this cushion my crown.
PRINCE. Your throne looks like a wooden stool, your golden scepter like a lead dagger, and your precious rich crown like a pathetic bald head.

FALSTAFF. Well, if the fire of grace hasn’t completely gone out of you, you’ll be moved now. Give me a cup of wine to make my eyes look red, so people will think I’ve been crying. I have to speak with great emotion, and I’ll do it in the ranting style of King Cambyses.
PRINCE. Well, here’s my bow.
FALSTAFF. And here’s my speech. Stand aside, my nobles.
HOSTESS. Oh Jesus, this is excellent fun, really!
FALSTAFF. Don’t cry, sweet Queen, because trickling tears are useless.
HOSTESS. Oh, by the Father, look how he keeps a straight face!
FALSTAFF. For God’s sake, lords, escort my sorrowful Queen away, because tears are blocking the floodgates of her eyes.
HOSTESS. Oh Jesus, he does it just like one of those trashy actors I’ve seen!

FALSTAFF. Quiet, good beer mug; quiet, good booze-pourer.—Harry, I wonder not only where you spend your time but also who you spend it with. The chamomile plant grows faster the more it’s trampled. But youth is the opposite: the more it’s wasted, the sooner it wears out. I know you’re my son partly because your mother says so and partly from my own opinion. But mostly it’s a wicked look in your eye and a foolish droop of your lower lip that convince me. So if you are my son, here’s the point: why, being my son, are you pointed at with scorn? Should the blessed sun in heaven play hooky and go eating blackberries? That question doesn’t need asking. Should the son of England become a thief and steal purses? That question does need asking. There’s a thing, Harry, that you’ve often heard of, and many in our country know it by the name of pitch. This pitch, as ancient writers say, leaves a stain; so does the company you keep. Harry, I’m not speaking to you now in drink, but in tears; not in pleasure, but in passion; not in words only, but in sorrows too. And yet there’s one good man I’ve often noticed in your company, but I don’t know his name.
PRINCE. What kind of man, if it please your Majesty?

FALSTAFF. A fine, stately man, really, and a stout one. He has a cheerful face, a pleasing eye, and a very noble bearing. I think he’s about fifty, or, by Our Lady, closer to sixty. And now I remember: his name is Falstaff. If that man is wicked, then he fools me, because, Harry, I see goodness in his looks. If a tree can be known by its fruit, as fruit is known by its tree, then I say it firmly: there’s goodness in that Falstaff. Keep him close, and banish the rest. And now tell me, you naughty rascal, tell me where you’ve been this past month?
PRINCE. Do you call that speaking like a king? You play me, and I’ll play my father.
FALSTAFF. You’re dethroning me? If you do it half as seriously and majestically, in both words and substance, then hang me up by the heels like a baby rabbit or a hare in a poultry shop.
PRINCE. Well, here I am, seated.
FALSTAFF. And here I stand. You be the judges, gentlemen.
PRINCE. Now, Harry, where have you come from?
FALSTAFF. My noble lord, from Eastcheap.
PRINCE. The complaints I hear about you are serious.
FALSTAFF. God’s blood, my lord, they’re lies.—No, I’ll entertain you as a young prince, believe me.

PRINCE. You swear, you graceless boy? From now on, never look at me again. You’ve been violently dragged away from grace. A devil haunts you in the shape of a fat old man. Your companion is a barrel of a man. Why do you spend time with that trunk full of diseases, that sifting bin of beastliness? Why with that swollen bundle of bloat, that huge leather jug of wine, that stuffed bag of guts? Why with that roasted Manningtree ox with the stuffing in its belly, that reverend Vice, that gray-haired sin, that father of thugs, that old fool? What is he good for, except tasting wine and drinking it? What is he neat and tidy at, except carving a chicken and eating it? What is he clever at, except trickery? What is he tricky at, except villainy? What is he villainous at? Everything. What is he worthy at? Nothing.
FALSTAFF. I wish your Grace would let me follow you. Whom does your Grace mean?
PRINCE. That wicked, disgusting misleader of youth, Falstaff, that old white-bearded Satan.
FALSTAFF. My lord, I know the man.
PRINCE. I know you do.

FALSTAFF. But if I said I knew more harm in him than in myself, I’d be saying more than I know. That he’s old—more’s the pity—his white hair proves. But that he’s a whoremonger, if you’ll pardon the word, I absolutely deny. If sweet wine with sugar is a crime, then God help the wicked! If being old and merry is a sin, then plenty of old innkeepers I know are damned. If being fat means being hated, then Pharaoh’s skinny cows deserve to be loved. No, my good lord. Banish Peto, banish Bardolph, banish Poins. But sweet Jack Falstaff, kind Jack Falstaff, loyal Jack Falstaff, brave Jack Falstaff—and all the braver for being old Jack Falstaff—don’t banish him from your Harry’s company. Don’t banish him from your Harry’s company. Banish plump Jack, and you banish the whole world.
PRINCE. I do. I will.
[Someone knocks at the door.]
[The Hostess, Francis and Bardolph exit.]
[Bardolph enters, running.]
BARDOLPH. Oh, my lord, my lord, the sheriff is at the door with a huge troop of watchmen.
FALSTAFF. Get out, you rascal! Let’s finish the play. I have a lot to say on behalf of that Falstaff.
[The Hostess enters in a hurry.]
HOSTESS. Oh Jesus, my lord, my lord—
PRINCE. Hey, hey, the devil’s riding a fiddlestick—what a fuss! What’s the matter?
HOSTESS. The sheriff and all the watch are at the door. They’ve come to search the house. Should I let them in?
FALSTAFF. Do you hear that, Hal? Never call a real gold coin a fake. You’re genuinely made of gold, even if you don’t look it.
PRINCE. And you’re a born coward, no instinct needed.

FALSTAFF. I deny your major premise. If you’ll turn the sheriff away, fine; if not, let him come in. If I don’t ride the hangman’s cart as well as the next man, damn my upbringing! I hope a noose will strangle me as quickly as anyone else.
PRINCE. Go hide behind the tapestry. The rest of you, go upstairs. Now, gentlemen, put on an honest face and a clear conscience.
FALSTAFF. I’ve had both, but they’ve expired, so I’ll go hide.
PRINCE. Call in the sheriff.
[Everyone exits except the Prince and Peto.]
[The Sheriff and the Carrier enter.]
Now, master sheriff, what do you want with me?
SHERIFF. First, forgive me, my lord. A public pursuit has chased certain men to this house.
PRINCE. What men?
SHERIFF. One of them is well known, my gracious lord. He’s a huge fat man.
CARRIER. As fat as butter.

PRINCE. I assure you the man isn’t here, because I’ve sent him on an errand of my own right now. And, sheriff, I give you my word that by lunchtime tomorrow I’ll send him to answer to you, or to anyone, for whatever he’s accused of. So let me ask you to leave the house.
SHERIFF. I will, my lord. Two gentlemen have lost three hundred marks in this robbery.
PRINCE. That may be. If he robbed these men, he’ll be held responsible. And so, goodbye.
SHERIFF. Good night, my noble lord.
PRINCE. I think it’s good morning by now, isn’t it?
SHERIFF. Yes, my lord, I think it’s about two o’clock.
[The Sheriff exits with the Carrier.]
PRINCE. This greasy rascal is as well known as St. Paul’s Cathedral. Go and call him out.
PETO. Falstaff!—He’s fast asleep behind the tapestry, snoring like a horse.
PRINCE. Listen to how hard he’s breathing. Search his pockets.
[He searches Falstaff’s pocket and finds some papers.]
What did you find?
PETO. Nothing but papers, my lord.
PRINCE. Let’s see what they are. Read them.
[He reads.]

PETO. Item: one roast chicken, at a cost of two shillings and twopence. Item: some sauce, at a cost of fourpence. Item: two whole gallons of sack, at a cost of five shillings and eightpence. Item: anchovies and more sack after supper, at a cost of two shillings and sixpence. Item: bread, at a cost of one halfpenny.

PRINCE. Outrageous! Only a halfpenny’s worth of bread to go with this unbearable amount of wine! Keep the rest of it safe. We’ll read it when we have more time. Let him sleep there till daylight. I’m going to court in the morning. We all have to go to war, and you’ll get an honorable post. I’ll get this fat rascal a command of foot soldiers, and I know marching two hundred and forty yards will kill him. The stolen money will be paid back with interest. Come see me early in the morning. And so, good morning, Peto.
PETO. Good morning, my good lord.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Bangor. A Room in the Archdeacon’s House
paragraphs: [Hotspur, Worcester, Mortimer and Glendower enter.]
MORTIMER. These promises look good, our allies are reliable, and our first steps give us every reason to hope for success.
HOTSPUR. Lord Mortimer, and cousin Glendower, won’t you sit down? And uncle Worcester—damn it! I’ve forgotten the map.

GLENDOWER. No, here it is. Sit, cousin Percy. Sit, good cousin Hotspur. Whenever King Henry of Lancaster speaks of you by that name, his cheek goes pale, and with a heavy sigh he wishes you were in heaven.
HOTSPUR. And he wishes you were in hell whenever he hears Owen Glendower mentioned.

GLENDOWER. I can’t blame him. When I was born, the face of the sky was full of fiery shapes, like blazing torches. And at my birth the whole frame and huge foundation of the Earth shook like a coward.
HOTSPUR. Well, it would have done the same at that moment if your mother’s cat had just had kittens, even if you’d never been born at all.
GLENDOWER. I’m telling you, the Earth shook when I was born.
HOTSPUR. And I’m telling you the Earth didn’t share my opinion, if you think it shook because it was afraid of you.
GLENDOWER. The whole sky was on fire, and the Earth trembled.

HOTSPUR. Oh, then the Earth shook because it saw the sky on fire, not because it feared your birth. Sick nature often bursts out in strange eruptions. The fertile Earth is often pinched and tormented by a kind of colic. Wild wind gets trapped inside her womb and struggles to get out. That shakes the old grandmother Earth and knocks down steeples and moss-covered towers. When you were born, our grandmother Earth had this disorder and shook in a fit.

GLENDOWER. Cousin, there aren’t many men I’d let contradict me like this. Allow me to tell you once more that when I was born, the face of the sky was full of fiery shapes. The goats ran down from the mountains, and the herds bellowed strangely across the frightened fields. These signs have marked me as extraordinary. Everything in my life shows that I’m not on the list of ordinary men. Where is there a man alive, anywhere inside the sea that batters the shores of England, Scotland and Wales, who can call me his pupil or claim to have taught me? Bring out any man born of a woman who can follow me down the hard paths of magic or keep up with me in deep experiments.
HOTSPUR. I don’t think any man speaks better Welsh nonsense than you. I’m going to dinner.
MORTIMER. Hush, cousin Percy, you’ll drive him mad.
GLENDOWER. I can summon spirits from the vast deep.
HOTSPUR. Well, so can I, or so can any man. But will they come when you call them?
GLENDOWER. Why, cousin, I can teach you how to command the devil.

HOTSPUR. And I can teach you, cousin, how to shame the devil—by telling the truth. Tell the truth, and shame the devil. If you have the power to raise him, bring him here, and I swear I have the power to shame him away. Oh, for as long as you live, tell the truth and shame the devil!
MORTIMER. Come on, come on, enough of this useless talk.

GLENDOWER. Three times Henry Bolingbroke has raised an army against my forces. Three times I’ve sent him back from the banks of the Wye and the sandy-bottomed Severn, with nothing to show for it and beaten by the weather.
HOTSPUR. Sent home without his boots, and in foul weather too! How on earth does he escape catching a fever, in the devil’s name?
GLENDOWER. Come, here’s the map. Shall we divide up our rights according to the three-way agreement we made?

MORTIMER. The archdeacon has divided it very evenly into three regions. England south and east of the Trent and the Severn is given to me. Everything to the west—Wales beyond the bank of the Severn and all the fertile land inside that border—goes to Owen Glendower. And to you, dear cousin, goes the rest, lying north of the Trent. Our three-part contracts are already drawn up. Once we’ve all sealed each other’s copies, which can be done tonight, we’ll set out tomorrow. You and I, cousin Percy, and my good Lord of Worcester will go to meet your father and the Scottish army at Shrewsbury, as arranged. My father-in-law Glendower isn’t ready yet, and we won’t need his help for another two weeks. [To Glendower.] In that time you can gather your tenants, friends and the neighboring gentlemen.

GLENDOWER. I’ll join you sooner than that, lords. I’ll escort your ladies when I come. You must slip away from them now without saying goodbye, because there would be an ocean of tears when you and your wives part.

HOTSPUR. It seems to me that my share, north of Burton here, isn’t as big as either of yours. Look how this river comes twisting in on me. It cuts a huge half-moon, a monstrous chunk, out of the best of my land. I’ll have the current dammed up at this spot. Then the smooth, silver Trent will run in a new channel, neat and even. It won’t wind in such a deep curve and rob me of such rich lowland here.
GLENDOWER. Not wind? It will, it must. You can see it does.
MORTIMER. Yes, but look how it runs its course and curves just as far up into my land on the other side. It cuts away as much of the land on the opposite bank as it takes from you on this side.
WORCESTER. Yes, but it would cost very little to dig a channel for it here. Then it would win this point of land on the north side and run straight and even.
HOTSPUR. That’s what I want. It won’t cost much to do it.
GLENDOWER. I won’t have it changed.
HOTSPUR. You won’t?
GLENDOWER. No, and neither will you.
HOTSPUR. Who’s going to tell me no?
GLENDOWER. Well, I am.
HOTSPUR. Then say it in Welsh, so I won’t understand you.

GLENDOWER. I can speak English as well as you can, my lord. I was brought up at the English court. While I was still young I set many English songs very beautifully to the harp, and gave the language a useful decoration—a talent no one has ever seen in you.

HOTSPUR. Indeed, and I’m glad of it with all my heart. I’d rather be a kitten crying “mew” than one of these rhyming ballad-peddlers. I’d rather hear a brass candlestick being turned on a lathe, or a dry wheel grinding on its axle. That wouldn’t set my teeth on edge nearly as much as fussy, prissy poetry. It’s like the forced gait of a hobbled old horse.
GLENDOWER. All right, you can have the Trent rerouted.

HOTSPUR. I don’t care. I’d give three times that much land to any friend who deserved it. But when it comes to a bargain, listen to me, I’ll argue over the ninth part of a hair. Are the contracts drawn up? Shall we go?

GLENDOWER. The moon is shining brightly, so you can leave tonight. I’ll hurry the clerk, and at the same time I’ll break the news of your departure to your wives. I’m afraid my daughter will go mad, she’s so devoted to her Mortimer.
[He exits.]
MORTIMER. Shame on you, cousin Percy, the way you contradict my father-in-law!

HOTSPUR. I can’t help it. Sometimes he makes me angry with his talk of the mole and the ant, the dreamer Merlin and his prophecies, a dragon and a fish without fins, a griffin with clipped wings and a molting raven, a crouching lion and a rearing cat.
