It’s so much rambling nonsense that it makes me lose my faith. Let me tell you—last night he kept me for at least nine hours, listing the names of all the devils who were his servants. I said “Hmm” and “Well, go on,” but I didn’t listen to a word. Oh, he’s as tiresome as a worn-out horse or a nagging wife. He’s worse than a smoky house. I’d rather live on cheese and garlic in a windmill far away than eat fine delicacies and have him talking to me in any summer house in Christendom.

MORTIMER. Honestly, he’s a worthy gentleman. He’s extremely well read and skilled in secret arts, brave as a lion, wonderfully friendly, and as generous as the mines of India. Shall I tell you something, cousin? He has great respect for your temper. He holds himself back from his natural impulses when you cross his mood—truly, he does. I promise you there’s no man alive who could provoke him the way you have without tasting danger and rebuke. But please, don’t do it often, I beg you.

WORCESTER. Honestly, my lord, you’re much too stubborn. Since you got here you’ve done enough to drive him completely out of patience. You really must learn to correct this fault, my lord. Sometimes it shows greatness, courage and noble spirit, and that’s the best credit it gives you. But it often comes across as harsh rage, bad manners, lack of self-control, pride, arrogance, conceit and scorn. Even the smallest of these, when it clings to a nobleman, loses him people’s hearts. It leaves a stain on the beauty of all his other qualities and robs them of the praise they deserve.
HOTSPUR. All right, I’ve been taught my lesson. May good manners bring you success! Here come our wives. Let’s say goodbye.
[Glendower enters with Lady Mortimer and Lady Percy.]
MORTIMER. This is the cruel spite that annoys me: my wife can’t speak English, and I can’t speak Welsh.
GLENDOWER. My daughter is crying. She won’t be parted from you. She wants to be a soldier too and go to the wars.
MORTIMER. Good father-in-law, tell her that she and my aunt Percy will follow soon under your escort.
[Glendower speaks to Lady Mortimer in Welsh, and she answers him in Welsh.]
GLENDOWER. She’s desperate about it, a stubborn, willful little hussy, someone no amount of persuasion can do any good with.
[Lady Mortimer speaks to Mortimer in Welsh.]
MORTIMER. I understand your looks. I know only too well that pretty Welsh you pour down from these overflowing eyes. If I weren’t ashamed, I’d answer you in the same language of tears.
[Lady Mortimer speaks to him again in Welsh.]

I understand your kisses, and you understand mine, and that’s a conversation full of feeling. But I’ll never slack off, my love, until I’ve learned your language. Your tongue makes Welsh as sweet as beautifully written songs, sung by a lovely queen in a summer garden, with enchanting runs of notes on her lute.
GLENDOWER. No, if you start to melt, she’ll go mad.
[Lady Mortimer speaks to Mortimer again in Welsh.]
MORTIMER. Oh, I’m completely ignorant in this!

GLENDOWER. She asks you to lie down on the soft rushes and rest your gentle head in her lap. She’ll sing the song you like and crown your eyelids with the god of sleep. She’ll charm your blood into a pleasant drowsiness, halfway between waking and sleeping. It will be like the hour between day and night, just before the sun’s heavenly team of horses begins its golden journey in the east.
MORTIMER. With all my heart, I’ll sit and hear her sing. By then, I think, our contract will be drawn up.
GLENDOWER. Do that. The musicians who will play for you are hanging in the air a thousand leagues from here, and they’ll be here at once. Sit down and listen.
HOTSPUR. Come, Kate, you’re an expert at lying down. Come on, quick, quick, so I can lay my head in your lap.
LADY PERCY. Go on, you silly goose.
[The music plays.]
HOTSPUR. Now I see the devil understands Welsh. No wonder he’s so moody. By Our Lady, he’s a good musician.
LADY PERCY. Then you should be completely musical, since you’re totally ruled by your moods. Lie still, you thief, and listen to the lady sing in Welsh.
HOTSPUR. I’d rather hear my hound bitch, Lady, howl in Irish.
LADY PERCY. Do you want your head cracked?
HOTSPUR. No.
LADY PERCY. Then be quiet.
HOTSPUR. I won’t do that either. Keeping still is a woman’s fault.
LADY PERCY. Now God help you!
HOTSPUR. Help me to the Welsh lady’s bed.
LADY PERCY. What was that?
HOTSPUR. Quiet, she’s singing.
[The lady sings a Welsh song.]
Come on, Kate, I want a song from you too.
LADY PERCY. Not from me, in good truth.

HOTSPUR. Not from me, in good truth! Good heavens, you swear like a candy-maker’s wife! “Not you, in good truth,” and “As true as I live,” and “As God shall mend me,” and “As sure as day.” You give such flimsy silk guarantees for your oaths, as if you’d never walked farther than the Finsbury fields. Kate, you’re a lady, so swear like one. Give me a good, mouth-filling oath. Leave “In truth,” and dainty gingerbread vows like that, to people in velvet trim and citizens in their Sunday best. Come on, sing.
LADY PERCY. I won’t sing.
HOTSPUR. Singing is the quickest way to become a tailor or a teacher of robins. If the contracts are drawn up, I’ll leave within two hours. So come in whenever you like.
[He exits.]

GLENDOWER. Come on, come on, Lord Mortimer. You’re as slow to leave as hot Lord Percy is eager to go. Our contract should be drawn up by now. We’ll just seal it and then get on our horses immediately.
MORTIMER. With all my heart.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — London. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [King Henry, Prince Henry and Lords enter.]
KING. Lords, leave us alone. The Prince of Wales and I need to have a private talk. But stay close by, because we’ll need you in a moment.
[The Lords exit.]

I don’t know whether God wants it this way because of some offense I’ve committed against Him. Perhaps in His secret judgment He means to breed revenge and a punishment for me out of my own blood. But the way you live your life makes me believe you were singled out as heaven’s hot vengeance and its whip, sent to punish my wrong steps. Otherwise, tell me this. How could such low, unruly desires, such poor, bare, lewd and petty doings, such empty pleasures and crude company as you’ve matched yourself with and grafted yourself onto, go along with the greatness of your blood? How could they stand level with your princely heart?

PRINCE. If it please your Majesty, I wish I could clear myself of every offense as plainly as I’m sure I can clear myself of many I’m accused of. Still, let me beg this much leniency. Many of the stories about me were invented by smiling flatterers and lowly gossipmongers, and great men often can’t help hearing them. Once those are disproved, I hope I may find pardon, through my honest submission, for the things that are true, where my youth has strayed into faults and disorder.

KING. God pardon you! Yet let me wonder at your tastes, Harry, which fly on a wing far away from the flight of all your ancestors. You’ve rudely lost your place in the Council, and your younger brother has taken it. You’ve become almost a stranger to the hearts of the whole court and of the princes of my blood. The hope and expectation of your future is ruined, and every man’s soul predicts your fall. If I had been as free with my presence, as cheap and overused in men’s eyes, as stale and common to low company, then public opinion, which helped me to the crown, would have stayed loyal to the man who held it. It would have left me in banishment without a reputation, a fellow of no note and no prospects. Because I was seldom seen, I couldn’t move without being stared at like a comet. Men would tell their children, “That’s him.” Others would say, “Where? Which one is Bolingbroke?” And then I stole all the graciousness of heaven and dressed myself in such humility that I plucked loyalty out of men’s hearts. I drew loud shouts and greetings from their mouths, even in the presence of the crowned King. That’s how I kept my person fresh and new. My presence was like a bishop’s robe, never seen without being marveled at. And so my public appearances, rare but rich, looked like a feast and won solemn respect through their rareness. The flighty King Richard ambled up and down with shallow jesters and hasty wits that flared up like kindling and burned out just as fast. He cheapened his royal status by mixing it with prancing fools. He let his great name be dragged down by their mockery. Against his own dignity, he lent his face to laugh at jeering boys and put up with the taunts of every beardless, vain wisecracker. He became a familiar sight in the common streets and handed himself over to popularity. So, because men’s eyes swallowed him up every day, they grew sick with too much honey and began to hate the taste of sweetness. A little more than a little of it is far too much. So when he had a real occasion to be seen, he was like the cuckoo in June: heard but not listened to. He was seen only by eyes that were sick and dull from seeing him so often. They gave him no special gaze, like the one turned on sun-like majesty when it shines rarely before admiring eyes. Instead they grew drowsy and drooped their eyelids. They slept in his face and gave him the sullen look that gloomy men give their enemies, being glutted, stuffed and full of him. And you, Harry, stand exactly on that same path. You’ve lost your princely privilege by mixing with lowlifes. There isn’t an eye that isn’t tired of the common sight of you, except mine. Mine has wanted to see more of you, and now it does what I wish it wouldn’t: it blinds itself with foolish tender tears.
PRINCE. From now on, my most gracious lord, I’ll be more like my true self.

KING. Just as you are now, Richard was then, when I landed from France at Ravenspurgh. And just as I was then, Percy is now. Now, I swear by my scepter and by my soul too, he has a worthier claim to the kingdom than you, who are only the shadow of an heir. With no right, and not even the appearance of right, he fills the fields of the realm with armor. He turns to face the lion’s armed jaws. And though he’s no older than you, he leads old lords and respected bishops into bloody battles and bruising combat. What undying honor he has won against the famous Douglas! Douglas’s great deeds, fierce raids and great name in arms give him the highest rank among all soldiers. They make him the chief military title in every kingdom that acknowledges Christ. Three times this Hotspur, a god of war in baby clothes, this infant warrior, has defeated the great Douglas in his campaigns. He captured him once, freed him, and made a friend of him. He did it to swell the roar of open defiance and to shake the peace and safety of our throne. And what do you say to this? Percy, Northumberland, his Grace the Archbishop of York, Douglas and Mortimer have joined together against us and are in arms. But why am I telling you this news? Why, Harry, do I tell you about my enemies, when you are my nearest and dearest enemy? You’re quite likely, out of slavish fear, low instincts and a fit of temper, to fight against me in Percy’s pay. You’d trail at his heels and bow whenever he frowns, just to show how far you’ve sunk.

PRINCE. Don’t think that; you won’t find it so. And God forgive those who have turned your Majesty’s good opinion so far away from me! I’ll win all this back on Percy’s head. At the end of some glorious day I’ll be bold enough to tell you that I am your son. On that day I’ll wear a garment made all of blood, and my face will be stained with a mask of blood. When it’s washed away, it will scrub off my shame along with it. And that will be the day, whenever it comes, when this child of honor and fame, this gallant Hotspur, this knight everyone praises, happens to meet your neglected Harry. I wish every honor sitting on his helmet were multiplied into crowds of honors, and my shames on my head doubled! For the time will come when I’ll make this northern youth trade his glorious deeds for my disgraces. Percy is only my agent, my good lord, buying up glorious deeds on my behalf. And I’ll call him to such a strict account that he’ll have to hand over every glory, yes, even the smallest honor of his life, or I’ll tear the account book out of his heart. I promise this here in God’s name. If it pleases Him that I carry it out, I beg your Majesty to let it heal the long-festering wounds of my wild living. If not, death cancels all debts, and I’ll die a hundred thousand deaths before I break the smallest part of this vow.
KING. A hundred thousand rebels die in that promise. You’ll have a command and my highest trust in this war.
[Sir Walter Blunt enters.]
What is it, good Blunt? You look like you’re in a great hurry.

BLUNT. So is the business I’ve come to tell you about. Lord Mortimer of Scotland has sent word that Douglas and the English rebels met at Shrewsbury on the eleventh of this month. If everyone keeps their promises, they’re as strong and frightening an army as ever threatened treachery in a kingdom.

KING. The Earl of Westmoreland set out today, and with him my son, Lord John of Lancaster, because this news is already five days old. Next Wednesday, Harry, you’ll set out. On Thursday we’ll march ourselves. Our meeting point is Bridgenorth. And, Harry, you’ll march through Gloucestershire. By that reckoning, given what we have to do, our combined forces will meet at Bridgenorth in about twelve days. Our hands are full of business. Let’s go. While men delay, the enemy grows fat on the advantage.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Eastcheap. A Room in the Boar’s Head Tavern
paragraphs: [Falstaff and Bardolph enter.]

FALSTAFF. Bardolph, haven’t I shrunk away terribly since that last job? Am I not wasting away? Am I not dwindling? Look, my skin hangs on me like an old lady’s loose gown. I’m shriveled like an old dried-up apple. Well, I’ll repent, and right away, while I’m still in some shape to do it. Soon I’ll lose heart, and then I won’t have the strength to repent. If I haven’t forgotten what the inside of a church looks like, then I’m a peppercorn or a brewer’s worn-out horse. The inside of a church! Bad company, villainous company, has been the ruin of me.
BARDOLPH. Sir John, you’re so fretful that you can’t live long.

FALSTAFF. Why, there it is. Come on, sing me a song, cheer me up. I used to be as virtuous as a gentleman needs to be, virtuous enough. I hardly ever swore. I gambled with dice no more than seven times—a week. I went to a whorehouse no more than once in a quarter—of an hour. I paid back money I borrowed—three or four times. I lived well and within bounds. And now I live out of all order, out of all bounds.
BARDOLPH. Well, you’re so fat, Sir John, that you have to be out of all bounds, out of all reasonable bounds, Sir John.
FALSTAFF. You fix your face, and I’ll fix my life. You’re our flagship, carrying the lantern on the stern, except yours is in your nose. You’re the Knight of the Burning Lamp.
BARDOLPH. Well, Sir John, my face doesn’t do you any harm.

FALSTAFF. No, I swear, I make as good use of it as many men do of a skull or a reminder of death. I never see your face without thinking of hellfire and of the rich man in the Bible who lived in purple, because there he is in his robes, burning, burning. If you had any leaning toward virtue at all, I’d swear by your face. My oath would be, “By this fire, which is God’s angel.” But you’re completely given over to sin. In fact, if it weren’t for the light in your face, you’d be the son of utter darkness. That night you ran up Gad’s Hill to catch my horse, I took you for a will-o’-the-wisp or a ball of wildfire, or money is worth nothing. Oh, you’re a never-ending victory parade, an everlasting bonfire! You’ve saved me a thousand marks in torches, walking with you at night from tavern to tavern. But the wine you’ve drunk at my expense would have bought me lights just as cheaply at the most expensive candlemaker’s in Europe. I’ve kept that salamander of yours in fire for these thirty-two years, and may God reward me for it!
BARDOLPH. By God’s blood, I wish my face were in your belly!
FALSTAFF. God have mercy! Then I’d be sure to get heartburn.
[The Hostess enters.]
Well, Dame Partlet the hen, have you found out yet who picked my pocket?

HOSTESS. Why, Sir John, what are you thinking, Sir John? Do you think I keep thieves in my house? I’ve searched, I’ve asked around, and so has my husband, man by man, boy by boy, servant by servant. Not a tenth of a hair was ever lost in my house before.
FALSTAFF. You’re lying, hostess. Bardolph got a shave here and lost plenty of hairs, and I swear my pocket was picked. Come on, you’re a woman, get out of here.
HOSTESS. Who, me? No, I defy you! By God’s light, I was never called that in my own house before.
FALSTAFF. Come on, I know you well enough.
HOSTESS. No, Sir John, you don’t know me, Sir John. I know you, Sir John. You owe me money, Sir John, and now you’re picking a fight to cheat me out of it. I bought you a dozen shirts for your back.
FALSTAFF. Cheap coarse linen, filthy cheap linen. I’ve given them away to bakers’ wives, and they’ve made flour sifters out of them.

HOSTESS. Now, as I’m an honest woman, that was fine Dutch linen at eight shillings a yard. You owe money here besides, Sir John, for your meals and drinks between meals, and money I lent you, twenty-four pounds.
FALSTAFF. He had his share of it; let him pay.
HOSTESS. Him? Oh dear, he’s poor, he has nothing.

FALSTAFF. What? Poor? Look at his face. What do you call rich? Let them mint coins out of his nose, let them mint coins out of his cheeks. I won’t pay a penny. What, are you going to treat me like a naive kid? Can’t I relax in my own inn without having my pocket picked? I’ve lost my grandfather’s signet ring, worth forty marks.
HOSTESS. Oh Jesus, I’ve heard the Prince tell him, I don’t know how often, that the ring was copper.
FALSTAFF. What? The Prince is a lowlife, a sneak. By God’s blood, if he were here and said that, I’d beat him like a dog.
[Prince Henry enters with Peto, marching. Falstaff meets them, playing on his staff as if it were a fife.]
What’s up, lad? Is that the way the wind is blowing, really? Do we all have to march?
BARDOLPH. Yes, two by two, like prisoners chained together on the way to Newgate.
HOSTESS. My lord, please, listen to me.
PRINCE. What do you have to say, Mistress Quickly? How is your husband? I like him a lot; he’s an honest man.
HOSTESS. My good lord, listen to me.
FALSTAFF. Please, leave her alone and listen to me.
PRINCE. What do you have to say, Jack?
FALSTAFF. The other night I fell asleep here behind the wall hanging and had my pocket picked. This house has turned into a whorehouse; they pick pockets.
PRINCE. What did you lose, Jack?
FALSTAFF. Would you believe me, Hal? Three or four bonds worth forty pounds each, and my grandfather’s signet ring.
PRINCE. A trifle, something worth about eight pennies.
HOSTESS. That’s what I told him, my lord, and I said I’d heard your Grace say so. And, my lord, he talks about you in the vilest way, foul-mouthed man that he is, and he said he would beat you.
PRINCE. What! He didn’t, did he?
HOSTESS. If he didn’t, then there’s no faith, truth or womanhood in me.

FALSTAFF. There’s no more faith in you than in a stewed prune, the kind they serve in whorehouses. There’s no more truth in you than in a hunted fox. And as for womanhood, Maid Marian, the shameless tart of the May games, would be a respectable deputy’s wife compared to you. Go on, you thing, go.
HOSTESS. Say it, what thing, what thing?
FALSTAFF. What thing? Why, a thing to thank God for.
HOSTESS. I’m no thing to thank God for, I’d have you know! I’m an honest man’s wife. And, knighthood aside, you’re a scoundrel to call me that.
FALSTAFF. And, womanhood aside, you’re a beast to say otherwise.
HOSTESS. Say it, what beast, you scoundrel, you?
FALSTAFF. What beast? Why, an otter.
PRINCE. An otter, Sir John? Why an otter?
FALSTAFF. Because she’s neither fish nor meat; a man doesn’t know where to have her.
HOSTESS. You’re an unfair man to say that. You or any man knows where to have me, you scoundrel, you.
PRINCE. You’re right, hostess, and he slanders you most grossly.
HOSTESS. He slanders you too, my lord. Just the other day he said you owed him a thousand pounds.
PRINCE. You there, do I owe you a thousand pounds?
FALSTAFF. A thousand pounds, Hal? A million. Your love is worth a million, and you owe me your love.
HOSTESS. No, my lord, he called you a lowlife and said he would beat you.
FALSTAFF. Did I, Bardolph?
BARDOLPH. Yes, Sir John, you did say so.
FALSTAFF. Yes, if he said my ring was copper.
PRINCE. I say it’s copper. Do you dare keep your word now?
FALSTAFF. Why, Hal, you know that as far as you’re just a man, I dare. But as far as you’re a prince, I fear you the way I fear the roar of a lion cub.
PRINCE. And why not the way you fear the lion?
FALSTAFF. The King himself is the one to be feared like the lion. Do you think I’ll fear you the way I fear your father? No, and if I do, I pray to God my belt breaks.

PRINCE. Oh, if it did, your guts would fall down around your knees! But, you there, there’s no room for faith, truth or honesty in that chest of yours; it’s all stuffed with guts. Accusing an honest woman of picking your pocket! Why, you bastard, you shameless, bloated rascal! If there was anything in your pocket besides tavern bills, notes from whorehouses, and one poor pennyworth of candy to help your wind, I’m a villain. That is, if your pocket was enriched with any other wrongs than these. And yet you’ll stand by your story, you won’t swallow an insult. Aren’t you ashamed?

FALSTAFF. Do you hear me, Hal? You know Adam fell in the state of innocence. So what is poor Jack Falstaff supposed to do in these days of wickedness? You can see I have more flesh than other men, and so more frailty. So you admit you picked my pocket?
PRINCE. It looks that way from the story.

FALSTAFF. Hostess, I forgive you. Go get breakfast ready, love your husband, keep an eye on your servants, take good care of your guests. You’ll find me open to any honest reason. You see I’m always calm and forgiving. No, please, go away now.
[The Hostess exits.]
Now, Hal, to the news from court. As for the robbery, lad, how has that been settled?
PRINCE. Oh, my sweet slab of beef, I always have to be your guardian angel. The money has been paid back.
FALSTAFF. Oh, I don’t like that paying back; it’s double the work.
PRINCE. I’m on good terms with my father now, and I can do anything.
FALSTAFF. Then the first thing you do, rob the treasury for me, and do it without even washing your hands.
BARDOLPH. Do it, my lord.
PRINCE. I’ve gotten you a command of foot soldiers, Jack.

FALSTAFF. I wish it had been a band of horsemen. Where can I find someone who steals well? Oh, for a fine thief of about twenty-two! I’m terribly short of supplies. Well, thank God for these rebels. They only offend the virtuous. I applaud them, I praise them.
PRINCE. Bardolph!
BARDOLPH. My lord?
PRINCE. Go take this letter to Lord John of Lancaster, my brother John. Take this one to my Lord of Westmoreland.
[Bardolph exits.]
Go, Peto, get to your horse, to your horse, because you and I still have thirty miles to ride before dinnertime.
[Peto exits.]

Jack, meet me tomorrow in the Temple hall at two in the afternoon. There you’ll learn your assignment and receive money and orders for your troops’ equipment. The country is on fire, and Percy stands high above us. Either we or they must end up lying low.
[He exits.]
FALSTAFF. Splendid words! What a fine world!—Hostess, bring my breakfast.—Oh, I wish this tavern could be my drum, so I could stay here while I go to war.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — The Rebel Camp near Shrewsbury
paragraphs: [Hotspur, Worcester and Douglas enter.]

HOTSPUR. Well said, my noble Scot. If telling the truth weren’t considered flattery in these refined times, the Douglas would earn so much praise that no soldier minted this season would be as widely valued around the world. By God, I can’t flatter. I scorn the tongues of smooth talkers. But no man holds a better place in my heart’s love than you do. Go on, hold me to my word; test me, my lord.
DOUGLAS. You are the king of honor. No man breathing on this earth is so powerful that I won’t defy him to his face.
HOTSPUR. Do that, and all will be well.
[A Messenger enters with letters.]
What letters do you have there? I can only thank you.
MESSENGER. These letters are from your father.
HOTSPUR. Letters from him! Why doesn’t he come himself?
MESSENGER. He can’t come, my lord. He’s seriously ill.
HOTSPUR. God’s wounds! How does he have the time to be sick at such a turbulent moment? Who is leading his army? Under whose command are they coming?
MESSENGER. His letters tell you his intentions, my lord, not I.
WORCESTER. Please tell me, is he confined to his bed?
MESSENGER. He was, my lord, for four days before I set out. And when I left, his doctors were very worried about him.
WORCESTER. I wish our affairs had been settled first, before this sickness struck him. His health was never more valuable than it is now.

HOTSPUR. Sick now? Fading now? This sickness infects the very lifeblood of our undertaking. It’s contagious; it has spread all the way to our camp. He writes to me here that he has an internal illness. He says his allies couldn’t be gathered so quickly through a deputy. And he didn’t think it right to hand such a dangerous and precious responsibility to anyone but himself. Still, he boldly advises us to push on with our small combined force and see how fortune treats us. As he writes, there’s no backing down now, because the King surely knows all our plans. What do you say to that?
WORCESTER. Your father’s illness is a crippling blow to us.

HOTSPUR. A dangerous wound, a whole limb chopped off—and yet, honestly, it isn’t! His absence now seems worse than it will turn out to be. Would it be wise to stake the entire wealth of all our forces on a single throw? To bet such a huge pot on the risky odds of one uncertain hour? It wouldn’t be wise. If we did, we’d be reaching the very bottom of our hope. We’d be at the very edge, the outermost limit, of all our fortunes.

DOUGLAS. True, that’s what we would do. As it is, we still have something sweet in reserve. We can spend boldly, counting on what’s still to come in. There’s comfort in having something to fall back on.
HOTSPUR. A meeting place, a home to run to, if the devil and bad luck glare menacingly at our affairs while they’re still young and untried.

WORCESTER. All the same, I wish your father were here. The nature and character of our attempt can’t tolerate any division. Some people who don’t know why he’s away will think he stayed home out of wisdom, loyalty to the King, and simple disapproval of what we’re doing. Think how such a belief could turn the tide among our nervous supporters. It could raise doubts about our cause. You know well that we, the attacking side, must stay clear of close scrutiny. We must block every peephole, every gap where the eye of reason might pry in on us. Your father’s absence pulls back a curtain. It shows the uninformed a kind of fear they never dreamed of before.

HOTSPUR. You’re going too far. I’d rather use his absence this way. It gives our great enterprise more glory, a better reputation and a bolder look than if the Earl were here. People will think that if we can raise an army against the kingdom without his help, then with his help we’ll turn it completely upside down. So all is still well; all our joints are still whole.
DOUGLAS. As well as anyone could wish. In Scotland nobody even speaks that word, fear.
[Sir Richard Vernon enters.]
HOTSPUR. My cousin Vernon! Welcome, by my soul.
VERNON. I pray to God my news deserves a welcome, my lord. The Earl of Westmoreland is marching this way with seven thousand men, and Prince John is with him.
HOTSPUR. No harm in that. What else?
VERNON. And I’ve also learned that the King himself has set out in person, or plans to head this way quickly, with a strong and mighty force.
HOTSPUR. He’ll be welcome too. Where’s his son, the quick-footed, wild Prince of Wales, and his buddies, who brushed the world aside and told it to go on its way?

VERNON. All equipped, all armed. They all wear plumes like ostriches, fluttering in the wind like eagles that have just bathed. They glitter in golden coats like statues of saints. They’re as full of spirit as the month of May and as gorgeous as the sun at midsummer. They’re as frisky as young goats and as wild as young bulls. I saw young Harry with his helmet on and his thigh armor on, gallantly armed. He rose from the ground like Mercury with his winged feet. He vaulted so easily into his saddle that it looked like an angel had dropped from the clouds. He was there to turn and wheel a fiery Pegasus and bewitch the world with his noble horsemanship.

HOTSPUR. No more, no more! This praise breeds fever in me, worse than the March sun. Let them come! They come decked out like sacrificial animals, and we’ll offer them, hot and bleeding, to the fire-eyed goddess of smoky war. Armored Mars will sit on his altar up to his ears in blood. I’m on fire to hear that this rich prize is so close and still not ours. Come, let me try out my horse. He’ll carry me like a thunderbolt against the chest of the Prince of Wales. Harry will meet Harry, hot horse against horse, and they won’t part until one drops down a corpse. Oh, if only Glendower had come!
VERNON. There’s more news. As I rode through Worcester I learned that he can’t gather his army for another two weeks.
DOUGLAS. That’s the worst news I’ve heard yet.
WORCESTER. Yes, by my faith, that has a chilling sound.
HOTSPUR. How many men might the King’s whole army add up to?
VERNON. Thirty thousand.

HOTSPUR. Let it be forty. With my father and Glendower both away, our own forces may be enough for such a great day. Come, let’s quickly review the troops. Doomsday is near; if we all die, let’s die cheerfully.
DOUGLAS. Don’t talk about dying. For the next half year I’m not afraid of death or of death’s hand.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — A public Road near Coventry
paragraphs: [Falstaff and Bardolph enter.]
FALSTAFF. Bardolph, go on ahead to Coventry and fill me a bottle of sherry. Our soldiers will march through. We’ll get to Sutton Coldfield tonight.
BARDOLPH. Will you give me money, captain?
FALSTAFF. Pay for it yourself, pay for it yourself.
BARDOLPH. This bottle comes to a ten-shilling coin.
FALSTAFF. If it does, keep it for your trouble. If it makes twenty of them, take them all; I’ll vouch for the coins. Tell my lieutenant Peto to meet me at the edge of town.
BARDOLPH. I will, captain. Goodbye.
[He exits.]

FALSTAFF. If I’m not ashamed of my soldiers, I’m a pickled fish. I’ve abused the King’s draft terribly. In exchange for a hundred and fifty soldiers, I’ve collected three hundred and some pounds. I drafted only solid householders and farmers’ sons. I went looking for engaged bachelors whose wedding banns had already been read twice. They were a batch of comfortable cowards who’d rather hear the devil than a drum. They feared the bang of a musket worse than a wounded bird or an injured wild duck does. I drafted only these soft milksops, with hearts in their bellies no bigger than pinheads, and they paid me to buy their way out of service. Now my whole company is made of standard-bearers, corporals, lieutenants and company officers. They’re wretches as ragged as Lazarus in a cheap wall painting, where the rich glutton’s dogs licked his sores. Some were never soldiers at all. They’re dishonest servants who were fired, younger sons of younger brothers, runaway bartenders and stable hands whose trade has dried up. They’re the parasites of a calm world and a long peace. They’re ten times more shamefully ragged than an old, frayed flag. These are the men I’ve used to fill the places of the ones who bought their way out. You’d think I had a hundred and fifty tattered prodigal sons just back from tending pigs and eating slop and husks. A crazy guy I met on the way told me I must have emptied all the gallows and drafted the dead bodies. No eye has ever seen such scarecrows. I won’t march through Coventry with them, and that’s final. And the villains walk with their legs wide apart, as if they still had shackles on. In fact, I got most of them out of prison. There isn’t a shirt and a half in my whole company. The half shirt is two napkins sewn together and thrown over the shoulders like a herald’s sleeveless coat. And the whole shirt, to tell the truth, was stolen from my innkeeper at Saint Albans, or from the red-nosed innkeeper of Daventry. But it doesn’t matter. They’ll find plenty of linen drying on every hedge.
[Prince Henry and the Lord of Westmoreland enter.]
PRINCE. What’s up, puffed-up Jack? What’s up, you stuffed quilt?
FALSTAFF. What, Hal! What’s up, you crazy joker? What the devil are you doing in Warwickshire? My good Lord of Westmoreland, I beg your pardon. I thought your honor was already at Shrewsbury.
WESTMORELAND. Honestly, Sir John, it’s past time I was there, and you too. But my troops are there already. The King, I can tell you, is expecting all of us. We must travel all night.
FALSTAFF. Tut, don’t worry about me. I’m as alert as a cat waiting to steal cream.
PRINCE. Yes, to steal cream, I’m sure, because your stealing has already churned you into butter. But tell me, Jack, whose men are these coming behind you?
FALSTAFF. Mine, Hal, mine.
PRINCE. I’ve never seen such pathetic wretches.
FALSTAFF. Tut, tut, they’re good enough to be tossed on a pike. Food for gunpowder, food for gunpowder. They’ll fill a mass grave as well as better men. Come on, man, they’re mortal men, mortal men.
WESTMORELAND. Yes, but, Sir John, I think they’re extremely poor and thin, too much like beggars.
FALSTAFF. Well, as for their poverty, I don’t know where they got that. And as for their thinness, I’m sure they never learned that from me.
PRINCE. No, I’ll swear to that, unless you call three inches of fat on the ribs thin. But hurry up. Percy is already on the battlefield.
[He exits.]
FALSTAFF. What, is the King already in camp?
WESTMORELAND. He is, Sir John. I’m afraid we’ll stay here too long.
[He exits.]
FALSTAFF. Well, the tail end of a fight and the start of a feast suit a sluggish fighter and a hungry guest.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — The Rebel Camp near Shrewsbury
paragraphs: [Hotspur, Worcester, Douglas and Vernon enter.]
HOTSPUR. We’ll fight him tonight.
WORCESTER. That can’t happen.
DOUGLAS. Then you give him the advantage.
VERNON. Not one bit.
HOTSPUR. Why do you say that? Isn’t he expecting reinforcements?
VERNON. So are we.
HOTSPUR. His are certain; ours are doubtful.
WORCESTER. Good nephew, take my advice. Don’t move tonight.
VERNON. Don’t, my lord.
DOUGLAS. That’s bad advice. You say it out of fear and cowardice.

VERNON. Don’t slander me, Douglas. By my life, I’ll gladly defend this with my life. When true honor calls me forward, I pay as little attention to weak fear as you do, my lord, or any Scot alive today. Let tomorrow’s battle show which of us is afraid.
DOUGLAS. Yes, or tonight’s.
VERNON. Agreed.
HOTSPUR. Tonight, I say.

VERNON. Come on, come on, it can’t be done. I’m amazed that men with your great experience of command don’t see the obstacles holding back our attack. Some of my cousin Vernon’s cavalry still haven’t arrived. Your uncle Worcester’s cavalry only got here today. Now their pride and spirit are asleep. Their courage is tamed and dulled by hard work, so that not one horse has even a quarter of its usual strength.
HOTSPUR. The enemy’s horses are the same, on the whole: worn out by the journey and brought low. Most of ours are well rested.
WORCESTER. The King’s army is bigger than ours. For God’s sake, nephew, wait until everyone arrives.
[A trumpet sounds, calling for talks.]
[Sir Walter Blunt enters.]
BLUNT. I come with generous offers from the King, if you’ll grant me a hearing and respect.

HOTSPUR. Welcome, Sir Walter Blunt. I wish to God you were on our side! Some of us love you well. And even those same people resent your great merits and good name, because you aren’t one of us and you stand against us like an enemy.

BLUNT. And God forbid I should ever stand any other way, as long as you stand against God’s anointed king, outside the law and true order. But to my mission. The King has sent me to learn the nature of your complaints. He wants to know why you summon such bold hostility out of the heart of civil peace, teaching his loyal land reckless cruelty. If the King has in any way forgotten your good services, which he admits are many, he asks you to name your complaints. Then, as quickly as possible, you’ll have what you want, with interest. And you’ll have a full pardon for yourself and for those you’ve led astray with your prompting.

HOTSPUR. The King is kind, and we know very well that the King knows when to promise and when to pay. My father, my uncle and I gave him the very crown he wears. Back then he didn’t have twenty-six men with him. He was sick in the world’s eyes, miserable and low, a poor, forgotten outlaw sneaking home. My father welcomed him to the shore. He heard him swear and vow to God that he came only to be Duke of Lancaster. He said he wanted to claim his inheritance and beg for peace, with innocent tears and earnest words. My father, moved by kindness and pity, swore to help him, and he did it too. Then the lords and barons of the realm saw that Northumberland supported him. So great and small came with hats off and knees bent. They met him in towns, cities and villages. They waited on him on bridges and lined the lanes. They laid gifts before him, offered him their oaths, and gave him their heirs as pages. They followed at his heels in glittering crowds. Then at once, as power knows its own strength, he climbed a little higher than the vow he made to my father. He made that vow while his fortunes were poor, on the bare shore at Ravenspurgh. And now, if you please, he takes it on himself to reform certain laws and strict decrees that weigh too heavily on the nation. He cries out against abuses and seems to weep over his country’s wrongs. With this face, this pretended look of justice, he won the hearts of everyone he fished for. He went further. He cut off the heads of all the favorites the absent King had left here as his deputies, while he was away in person fighting the war in Ireland.
BLUNT. Tut, I didn’t come here to listen to this.

HOTSPUR. Then to the point. Shortly afterward he overthrew the King. Soon after that he took his life. Right on the heels of that, he taxed the whole country. To make it worse, he let his kinsman March be held captive in Wales, left there without ransom and abandoned. And if everyone had his rightful place, March would actually be his king. He insulted me after my fortunate victories. He tried to trap me with spies. He scolded my uncle and drove him from the Council table. In a rage he banished my father from court. He broke oath after oath and committed wrong after wrong. In the end he drove us to raise this army for our safety. He also drove us to look closely into his claim to the throne, and we now find it too crooked to last long.
BLUNT. Shall I take this answer back to the King?

HOTSPUR. No, Sir Walter. We’ll consider it for a while. Go to the King, and let him give some hostage as a guarantee of a safe return. Early in the morning my uncle will bring him our intentions. And so, goodbye.
BLUNT. I wish you would accept his mercy and friendship.
HOTSPUR. And maybe we will.
BLUNT. I pray to God you do.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — York. A Room in the Archbishop’s Palace
paragraphs: [The Archbishop of York and Sir Michael enter.]

ARCHBISHOP. Hurry, good Sir Michael. Carry this sealed letter with lightning speed to the Lord Marshal. Take this one to my cousin Scroop, and the rest to the people they’re addressed to. If you knew how important they are, you would hurry.
SIR MICHAEL. My good lord, I can guess what they say.

ARCHBISHOP. You probably do. Tomorrow, good Sir Michael, is a day when the fortunes of ten thousand men will be put to the test. For, sir, as I truly understand it, the King, with a mighty army raised in haste, is meeting Lord Harry at Shrewsbury. And I fear, Sir Michael, for several reasons. Northumberland is sick, and his forces were the largest share. Owen Glendower is absent too, and he was counted a major strength among them. He isn’t coming, because he’s been overruled by prophecies. So I fear Percy’s army is too weak to risk an immediate battle with the King.
SIR MICHAEL. Why, my good lord, you don’t need to be afraid. Douglas is there, and Lord Mortimer.
ARCHBISHOP. No, Mortimer isn’t there.
SIR MICHAEL. But Mordake is there, and Vernon, and Lord Harry Percy. My Lord of Worcester is there too, with a troop of brave warriors and noble gentlemen.

ARCHBISHOP. That’s true. But the King has gathered the very best men in the land: the Prince of Wales, Lord John of Lancaster, the noble Westmoreland and the warlike Blunt. He also has many more rivals in honor and valued men with reputation and command in war.
SIR MICHAEL. Don’t doubt it, my lord, they’ll be well matched.

ARCHBISHOP. I hope so, but it’s necessary to fear. And to head off the worst, Sir Michael, hurry. If Lord Percy doesn’t succeed, the King means to visit us before he disbands his army. He has heard about our alliance, and it’s only sensible to build up our strength against him. So hurry. I must go and write again to other friends. And so, goodbye, Sir Michael.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — The King’s Camp near Shrewsbury
paragraphs: [King Henry, Prince Henry, Lancaster, Sir Walter Blunt and Sir John Falstaff enter.]
KING. How bloody the sun looks as it begins to peek over that massive hill! The day looks pale at the sun’s sickly mood.
PRINCE. The south wind is playing the trumpet for the sun’s intentions. With its hollow whistling in the leaves, it predicts a storm and a blustery day.
KING. Then let it sympathize with the losers, because nothing can seem bad to those who win.
[The trumpet sounds.]
[Worcester and Vernon enter.]

Well now, my Lord of Worcester! It isn’t right that you and I should meet on terms like these. You have betrayed our trust. You made us take off our comfortable robes of peace and squeeze our old limbs into harsh steel armor. This isn’t right, my lord, this isn’t right. What do you say about it? Will you untie this ugly knot of hateful war once more? Will you return to your obedient orbit around me, where you used to give off a fair and natural light? Will you stop being a stray meteor, a terrifying omen and a sign of evil let loose upon future generations?
WORCESTER. Listen to me, my king. For my own part, I’d be happy to spend the last stretch of my life in quiet hours. I swear I haven’t gone looking for this day of conflict.
KING. You haven’t looked for it? Then how did it come about?
FALSTAFF. Rebellion was lying in his path, and he found it.
PRINCE. Quiet, you chattering jackdaw, quiet!

WORCESTER. Your Majesty chose to turn your favor away from me and all our family. And yet I must remind you, my lord, that we were the first and closest of your friends. For your sake, in Richard’s time, I broke my staff of office. I rode day and night to meet you on the road and kiss your hand. Back then you were nowhere near as strong or fortunate in rank and reputation as I was. It was me, my brother and his son who brought you home and boldly faced down the dangers of the time. You swore to us, and you swore that oath at Doncaster, that you had no plans against the state. You claimed nothing more than your newly inherited right, the seat of Gaunt, the dukedom of Lancaster. We swore to help you with that. But soon fortune came pouring down on your head like rain. A flood of greatness fell on you, partly through our help and partly because the King was away. It came also from the wrongs of a reckless time and the injuries you seemed to have suffered. And contrary winds kept the King so long in his unlucky Irish wars that everyone in England believed he was dead. From this swarm of convenient opportunities, you let yourself be quickly tempted to grab total power into your own hands. You forgot the oath you made to us at Doncaster. And though we fed you, you treated us the way that rude creature, the cuckoo’s chick, treats the sparrow. You took over our nest and grew so huge on our feeding that even our love didn’t dare come near you, for fear of being swallowed. So we were forced to fly quickly out of your sight for our own safety and raise this army. Now we stand against you by means that you yourself forged against yourself. You did it with unkind treatment, threatening looks, and the breaking of every promise and pledge you swore to us when your venture was young.

KING. Yes, you have spelled these things out. You’ve proclaimed them at market crosses and read them in churches. You do it to trim the garment of rebellion with some pretty color that will please the eye of fickle turncoats and poor malcontents. Those people gape and rub their elbows with glee at news of chaotic change. Rebellion has never lacked such watercolors to paint over its cause. Nor has it lacked sulky beggars starving for a time of total havoc and confusion.

PRINCE. In both your armies, many a soul will pay dearly for this clash if they ever meet in battle. Tell your nephew that the Prince of Wales joins the whole world in praising Henry Percy. I swear by my hopes of heaven, if you leave this rebellion out of his account, I don’t think there is a braver gentleman alive. No one is more actively brave or bravely young, more daring or more bold, to grace this modern age with noble deeds. For my part, and I say it to my shame, I have been a truant from chivalry. I hear that’s how he regards me too. Yet I say this before my father’s Majesty: I am willing to let him have the advantage of his great name and reputation. And to save blood on both sides, I will try my luck against him in single combat.

KING. And, Prince of Wales, we would dare to risk you in that fight, even though countless considerations weigh against it.—No, good Worcester, no. We love our people well. We even love those who have been misled into joining your nephew’s side. If they accept our offer of pardon, then he, and they, and you, yes, every man, shall be my friend again, and I’ll be his. So tell your nephew that, and then bring me word of what he’ll do. But if he won’t surrender, punishment and dreadful correction are on our side, and they will do their job. So, go. We won’t be bothered with a reply now. We are making a fair offer, so consider it wisely.
[Worcester exits with Vernon.]
PRINCE. It won’t be accepted, I’d bet my life on it. Douglas and Hotspur together are confident enough to take on the whole world in arms.
KING. So go, every leader, to his post. As soon as we get their answer, we will attack them. And may God help us, since our cause is just!
[The King, Blunt and Prince John exit.]
FALSTAFF. Hal, if you see me knocked down in the battle, stand over me and defend me. That’s what a friend does.
PRINCE. Only a colossus could straddle you to do you that favor. Say your prayers, and goodbye.
FALSTAFF. I wish it were bedtime, Hal, and everything were fine.
PRINCE. Well, you owe God a death.
[He exits.]

FALSTAFF. It isn’t due yet. I’d hate to pay Him before the payment date. Why should I be so eager to settle with someone who isn’t asking me? Well, it doesn’t matter, honor spurs me on. Yes, but what if honor spurs me off, out of this life, when I charge in? What then? Can honor set a broken leg? No. Or an arm? No. Or take away the pain of a wound? No. Then honor has no skill at surgery? No. What is honor? A word. What is in that word, “honor”? What is that “honor”? Air. A fine bargain! Who has it? The man who died on Wednesday. Does he feel it? No. Does he hear it? No. Then it can’t be sensed? Not by the dead, no. But won’t it live on with the living? No. Why not? Slander won’t allow it. So I’ll have none of it. Honor is nothing but a painted coat of arms carried at a funeral. And that’s the end of my catechism.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — The Rebel Camp
paragraphs: [Worcester and Vernon enter.]
WORCESTER. Oh no, Sir Richard, my nephew must not hear about the King’s generous and kind offer.
VERNON. It would be best if he did.

WORCESTER. Then we are all ruined. It’s not possible, it can’t be, that the King would keep his word and love us. He will always suspect us. He’ll find a time to punish this offense by charging us with other faults. Suspicion will watch us all our lives with a hundred eyes. Traitors are trusted no more than the fox. However tame it is, however pampered and locked up, it will still have some wild trick from its ancestors. However we look, sad or cheerful, people will misread our faces. We’ll be like oxen fed in a stall: the better we’re looked after, the nearer we are to slaughter. My nephew’s crime may well be forgotten. He has the excuse of youth and hot blood, and a nickname that gives him license: a harebrained Hotspur, ruled by his temper. All his offenses will land on my head and on his father’s. We trained him up to this. Since he learned his corruption from us, we, as the source of it all, will pay for it all. So, good kinsman, don’t let Harry know about the King’s offer, whatever happens.
VERNON. Tell him whatever you want, and I’ll back you up. Here comes your nephew.
[Hotspur and Douglas enter, with officers and soldiers behind them.]
HOTSPUR. My uncle is back. Release my Lord of Westmoreland. Uncle, what’s the news?
WORCESTER. The King will offer you battle right away.
DOUGLAS. Send him our defiance by the Lord of Westmoreland.
HOTSPUR. Lord Douglas, go and tell him so yourself.
DOUGLAS. Indeed I will, and very gladly.
[He exits.]
WORCESTER. The King shows no sign of mercy.
HOTSPUR. Did you beg for any? God forbid!

WORCESTER. I calmly told him about our complaints and about his oath-breaking. He fixed that by now swearing that he never broke his oath. He calls us rebels and traitors. He means to punish that hateful name in us with his proud armies.
[Douglas enters.]
DOUGLAS. Arm yourselves, gentlemen, to arms! I have thrown a bold defiance in King Henry’s teeth. Westmoreland, who was our hostage, carried it to him. That can only bring him on us quickly.
WORCESTER. The Prince of Wales stepped forward in front of the King, and, nephew, he challenged you to single combat.

HOTSPUR. Oh, I wish the quarrel rested on our heads alone! I wish no man had to fight himself out of breath today except me and Harry Monmouth! Tell me, tell me, how did he make his challenge? Did it seem scornful?

VERNON. No, I swear by my soul. I’ve never in my life heard a challenge made more modestly. It was like a brother daring a brother to a friendly match and test of arms. He gave you every respect a man is owed. He decorated your praises with a princely tongue. He listed your merits like a history book, always making you greater than his praise of you, and calling his own praise too small for your worth. And, which truly suited a prince, he spoke about himself with a blush. He scolded his own wasted youth so gracefully that he seemed to have a double gift, teaching and learning at the same moment. Then he stopped. But let me tell the world this: if he survives the hatred of this day, England has never had so sweet a hope, or one so badly misjudged because of his wild behavior.

HOTSPUR. Cousin, I think you’ve fallen in love with his foolishness. I never heard of any prince so wild and unrestrained. But let him be whatever he is. Before nightfall, I’ll embrace him with a soldier’s arm so that he shrinks under my courtesy. Arm, arm quickly! And, comrades, soldiers, friends, you had better think about what you have to do yourselves. I don’t have the gift of speech to stir your blood with persuasion.
[A messenger enters.]
MESSENGER. My lord, here are letters for you.

HOTSPUR. I can’t read them now.— Oh, gentlemen, life is short! Even if life rode on the hand of a clock and ended when the hour came round, it would still be too long to spend that short time shamefully. If we live, we live to trample on kings. If we die, what a brave death, when princes die with us! Now, as for our consciences, taking up arms is honorable when the reason for doing so is just.
[Another messenger enters.]
MESSENGER. My lord, get ready. The King is advancing quickly.

HOTSPUR. I thank him for cutting my speech short, because I’m no talker. Just this: let every man do his best. And here I draw a sword whose steel I intend to stain with the best blood I can find in the risks of this dangerous day. Now, Esperance! Percy! And forward. Sound all the noble instruments of war. And to that music let us all embrace. For I’d bet heaven against earth that some of us will never get to do such a courtesy a second time.
[The trumpets sound. They embrace and exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — Plain between the Camps
paragraphs: [The King enters with his army. The call to battle sounds. Then Douglas and Sir Walter Blunt enter.]
BLUNT. What’s your name, you who block my way like this in battle? What honor do you hope to win from my head?
DOUGLAS. Then know that my name is Douglas. I’m hunting you this way in battle because some people tell me you’re a king.
BLUNT. They’re telling you the truth.
DOUGLAS. The Lord of Stafford paid dearly today for looking like you. Instead of you, King Harry, this sword finished him off. It will do the same to you unless you surrender as my prisoner.
BLUNT. I wasn’t born to surrender, you proud Scot. And you will find a king here who will avenge Lord Stafford’s death.
[They fight, and Blunt is killed.]
[Hotspur enters.]
HOTSPUR. Oh Douglas, if you’d fought like this at Holmedon, I would never have triumphed over a Scot.
DOUGLAS. It’s all over, it’s all won. Here lies the King, dead.
HOTSPUR. Where?
DOUGLAS. Here.
HOTSPUR. This one, Douglas? No, I know this face very well. He was a brave knight, and his name was Blunt. He was dressed to look just like the King himself.
DOUGLAS. May foolishness follow your soul wherever it goes! You paid too high a price for a borrowed title. Why did you tell me you were a king?
HOTSPUR. The King has many men marching in his coats of arms.
DOUGLAS. Now, by my sword, I will kill all his coats. I’ll murder his whole wardrobe, piece by piece, until I meet the King.
HOTSPUR. Come on, let’s go! Our soldiers are well placed to win the day.
[They exit.]
[Battle calls. Falstaff enters alone.]

FALSTAFF. Though I could escape paying the bill in London, I’m afraid of the shot here. There’s no running up a tab here except on your skull.—Wait! Who are you? Sir Walter Blunt. There’s honor for you. That’s no vanity! I’m as hot as molten lead, and as heavy too. God keep lead bullets out of me, I don’t need any more weight than my own guts. I’ve led my ragamuffins where they’ve been shot full of holes. There aren’t three of my hundred and fifty left alive. And those few are headed for the edge of town to beg for the rest of their lives. But who’s coming here?
[Prince Henry enters.]

PRINCE. What, are you standing around doing nothing? Lend me your sword. Many noblemen lie stiff and dead under the hooves of boasting enemies, and their deaths are not yet avenged. Please, lend me your sword.
FALSTAFF. Oh Hal, please let me catch my breath a moment. Turk Gregory, that warlike pope, never did such deeds in battle as I have done today. I have paid Percy back, I’ve made sure of him.
PRINCE. He is sure, all right, and alive to kill you. Please, lend me your sword.
FALSTAFF. No, by God, Hal, if Percy is alive you’re not getting my sword. But take my pistol if you want.
PRINCE. Give it to me. What, is it in its holster?
FALSTAFF. Yes, Hal, it’s hot, it’s hot. There’s something in there that will sack a city.
[The Prince pulls out a bottle of sack.]
PRINCE. What, is this a time for joking and fooling around?
[He throws it at Falstaff and exits.]

FALSTAFF. Well, if Percy is alive, I’ll pierce him. If he comes my way, fine. If he doesn’t, and I go into his path willingly, let him slice me up like a grilled steak. I don’t like the kind of grinning honor Sir Walter has. Give me life. If I can save it, fine. If not, honor comes without my looking for it, and that’s the end of it.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — Another Part of the Field
paragraphs: [Battle calls. Soldiers rush across. King Henry, Prince Henry, Lancaster and Westmoreland enter.]
KING. Please, Harry, withdraw. You’re bleeding too much. Lord John of Lancaster, go with him.
LANCASTER. Not me, my lord, unless I were bleeding too.
PRINCE. I beg your Majesty, go back to the front, or your retreat will alarm your friends.
KING. I will. My Lord of Westmoreland, take him to his tent.
WESTMORELAND. Come, my lord, I’ll take you to your tent.

PRINCE. Take me, my lord? I don’t need your help. God forbid a shallow scratch should drive the Prince of Wales from a field like this one. Here bloodstained nobles lie trampled, and the rebels’ weapons triumph in slaughter!
LANCASTER. We’re resting too long. Come, cousin Westmoreland, our duty lies this way. For God’s sake, come.
[Lancaster and Westmoreland exit.]
PRINCE. By heaven, you fooled me, Lancaster. I didn’t think you had that kind of spirit in you. Before, I loved you as a brother, John, but now I value you as much as my own soul.
KING. I saw him hold Lord Percy off at sword’s point with more vigor than I expected from such an inexperienced young warrior.
PRINCE. Oh, this boy puts courage into all of us!
[He exits.]
[Douglas enters.]
DOUGLAS. Another king! They keep growing back like the Hydra’s heads. I am the Douglas, and I am death to everyone who wears those colors. Who are you, pretending to be a king?

KING. I am the King himself. And it grieves me deeply, Douglas, that you have met so many of my stand-ins and not the real King. I have two sons searching the battlefield for Percy and for you. But since you’ve had the luck to run into me, I will test you. So defend yourself.
DOUGLAS. I’m afraid you are another fake. And yet, I swear, you carry yourself like a king. But whoever you are, I’m sure you’re mine, and this is how I win you.
[They fight. The King is in danger, and Prince Henry enters.]

PRINCE. Hold your head up, you vile Scot, or you’ll probably never hold it up again! The spirits of brave Shirley, Stafford and Blunt are in my arms. It is the Prince of Wales who threatens you, and he never makes a promise he doesn’t mean to keep.
[They fight. Douglas runs away.]
Cheer up, my lord. How are you, your Grace? Sir Nicholas Gawsey has sent for help, and so has Clifton. I’ll go to Clifton right away.
KING. Wait and catch your breath a moment. You have won back the reputation you had lost. With this brave rescue you’ve brought me, you have shown that you do care about my life.

PRINCE. Oh God, the people who said I was waiting for your death did me a great wrong. If that were true, I could have just left Douglas’s insolent hand alone to do its work on you. It would have ended you as quickly as all the poisons in the world, and it would have saved your son the trouble of treachery.
KING. Hurry to Clifton. I’ll go to Sir Nicholas Gawsey.
[He exits.]
[Hotspur enters.]
HOTSPUR. Unless I’m mistaken, you are Harry Monmouth.
PRINCE. You say that as if I would deny my own name.
HOTSPUR. My name is Harry Percy.

PRINCE. Then I see a very brave rebel by that name. I am the Prince of Wales. And don’t think, Percy, that you will share glory with me any longer. Two stars can’t move in the same orbit. And one England can’t put up with two rulers, Harry Percy and the Prince of Wales.
HOTSPUR. And it won’t have to, Harry, because the hour has come to end one of us. I only wish to God your name as a fighter were as great as mine is now!
PRINCE. I’ll make it greater before I leave you. I’ll clip every honor that’s budding on your helmet and make it into a garland for my own head.
HOTSPUR. I can’t stand your bragging any longer.
[They fight.]
[Falstaff enters.]
FALSTAFF. Nicely done, Hal! Go at him, Hal! No, I can tell you, you won’t find any child’s game here.
[Douglas enters. He fights with Falstaff, who falls down as if he were dead. Douglas exits. The Prince kills Hotspur.]

HOTSPUR. Oh Harry, you have robbed me of my youth! I can bear losing my fragile life better than losing the proud titles you have won from me. They wound my mind worse than your sword wounds my flesh. But thoughts are slaves to life, and life is time’s fool. And time, which oversees the whole world, must come to an end too. Oh, I could predict the future, except that death’s cold, earthy hand is lying on my tongue. No, Percy, you are dust, and food for—
[He dies.]

PRINCE. For worms, brave Percy. Farewell, great heart! Badly woven ambition, how much you’ve shrunk! When this body held a living spirit, a whole kingdom was too small to contain it. But now two paces of the lowest dirt are room enough. The earth that holds you dead doesn’t hold a braver gentleman alive. If you could feel my courtesy, I wouldn’t show my admiration so openly. But let my plumes cover your mangled face. And on your behalf, I’ll thank myself for performing these kind last rites. Goodbye, and take your praise with you to heaven! Let your disgrace sleep with you in the grave, and let it not be remembered in your epitaph!
[He sees Falstaff on the ground.]

What, old friend, couldn’t all this flesh hold on to a little bit of life? Poor Jack, goodbye! I could have more easily lost a better man. Oh, I would miss you badly if I were still in love with foolish pleasures. Death hasn’t killed so fat a deer today, though it has killed many dearer ones in this bloody battle. I’ll see you disemboweled soon, like a deer after the hunt. Until then, lie here in your blood beside noble Percy.
[He exits.]
[Falstaff gets up.]

FALSTAFF. Disemboweled! If you gut me today, I’ll give you permission to salt me and eat me tomorrow too. God’s blood, it was time to fake it, or that hot-tempered savage Scot would have paid me off in full. Fake? I’m lying, I’m no fake. To die is to be a fake, because a man without a man’s life is only an imitation of a man. But to fake dying, when a man stays alive by doing it, is not to be a fake at all. It is the true and perfect image of life itself. The better part of courage is good judgment, and with that better part I have saved my life. Damn it, I’m afraid of this hothead Percy, even though he’s dead. What if he’s faking too, and gets up? Honestly, I’m afraid he’d turn out to be the better faker. So I’ll make sure of him, yes, and I’ll swear I killed him. Why couldn’t he get up just like I did? Nothing can prove me wrong except eyewitnesses, and nobody sees me. So, you, with a new wound in your thigh, come along with me.
[He picks Hotspur up and carries him on his back.]
[Prince Henry and Lancaster enter.]
PRINCE. Come on, brother John, you’ve blooded your untried sword very bravely.
LANCASTER. But wait, who do we have here? Didn’t you tell me this fat man was dead?

PRINCE. I did. I saw him dead, not breathing and bleeding on the ground.—Are you alive? Or is it an illusion playing tricks on our eyes? Please, speak. We won’t trust our eyes without our ears. You are not what you seem.

FALSTAFF. No, that’s for sure, I’m not two men in one. But if I’m not Jack Falstaff, then I’m a jackass. There’s Percy! [He throws the body down.] If your father wants to give me some honor, fine. If not, let him kill the next Percy himself. I expect to be made either an earl or a duke, I promise you.
PRINCE. What? I killed Percy myself, and I saw you dead.

FALSTAFF. Did you? Lord, Lord, how full of lying this world is! I admit I was down and out of breath, and so was he. But we both got up at the same instant and fought for a long hour by the Shrewsbury clock. If people believe me, good. If not, let the ones who should reward bravery carry the sin on their own heads. I’ll swear on my deathbed that I gave him this wound in the thigh. If the man were alive and denied it, God’s wounds, I’d make him eat a piece of my sword.
LANCASTER. This is the strangest story I have ever heard.
PRINCE. This is the strangest fellow, brother John.—Come on, carry your baggage proudly on your back. As for me, if a lie can do you some good, I’ll decorate it with the nicest words I have.
[Trumpets sound a retreat.]
The trumpet is sounding the retreat, so the day is ours. Come, brother, let’s go to the highest part of the battlefield to see which of our friends are alive and which are dead.
[Prince Henry and Lancaster exit.]

FALSTAFF. I’ll follow along, as they say, for my reward. Whoever rewards me, may God reward him! If I become great, I’ll become smaller, because I’ll take laxatives, give up sack, and live decently, the way a nobleman should.
[He exits, carrying off the body.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — Another Part of the Field
paragraphs: [The trumpets sound. King Henry, Prince Henry, Lancaster, Westmoreland and others enter, with Worcester and Vernon as prisoners.]

KING. This is how rebellion always gets punished. Evil-minded Worcester, didn’t we send all of you mercy, pardon and loving terms? And you dared to twist our offers into the opposite? You abused the trust your nephew put in you? Three knights on our side were killed today, along with a noble earl and many others. They would be alive this very hour if you had carried our messages honestly between the armies, like a Christian.
WORCESTER. I did what I did because my own safety forced me to. And I accept this fate patiently, since it falls on me and I can’t avoid it.
KING. Take Worcester away to be executed, and Vernon too. We will think further about the other offenders.
[Worcester and Vernon exit under guard.]
How is the battle going?

PRINCE. The noble Scot, Lord Douglas, saw the day’s luck turn completely against him. He saw noble Percy dead and all his men running in fear, so he fled with the rest. He fell off a hill and was so badly hurt that the men chasing him caught him. The Douglas is at my tent, and I beg your Grace to let me decide what to do with him.
KING. With all my heart.

PRINCE. Then, brother John of Lancaster, this honorable act of generosity will belong to you. Go to the Douglas and set him free to go wherever he likes, with no ransom. The courage he showed today against our helmets has taught us to value such noble deeds, even in our enemies.
LANCASTER. I thank your Grace for this great courtesy, which I will pass on to him right away.

KING. Then all that’s left is to divide our forces. You, my son John, and my cousin Westmoreland, will head toward York as fast as you can. There you’ll meet Northumberland and Archbishop Scroop, who we hear are busy raising arms. I and you, my son Harry, will go toward Wales to fight Glendower and the Earl of March. Rebellion in this country will lose its power if it meets another defeat like today’s. And since this business has gone so well, let’s not stop until everything that is ours has been won back.
[They exit.]
